Consideration of the motion of the right hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) for the second reading of Bill No. 75, Military Service Act, 1917, resumed from Monday, June 18.

Mr. Speaker, having occupied the position of Minister of Militia for a considerable time during the war, -tl am more or less familiar with matters concerning recruiting, how it is carried on, and why it fell off, and possibly I may be in a position to give some suggestions as to what in my opinion, at all events, would be the proper method to adopt for the future. I may point out that I gave notice on May 8, that I would move the following resolution.
On the first opportunity on going into Committee of Supply, I shall move:-That in the opinion of this House the hest interests of Canada, of the Empire, and of humanity, will be served by the application of the Militia Act, or by other action, to raise troops for compulsory overseas service.
This was not intended as a "want of confidence" motion, although I wrote the Prime Minister on the 17th October last strongly recommending compulsory service. I spoke about it at meetings all over the country during October, and I have consistently advocated it ever since. If the Prime Minister has no objection, I shall read the letter which I sent him on the 17th October last.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have no objection.

The letter reads as follow:
October 17, 1916. Dear Sir Robert,-	.
Regarding Compulsory Service.
The following are my own personal views and I alone wish to be held responsible for them; that is, I do not wish to profess to express any one's views but my own; others, however, let me hope, may hold the same ideas.
As you ara aware, I have always been in favour of universal training and service. If the Federal Government had control of the schools and educational institutions of the country generally, I would, as I have frequently stated, so far as I am personally concerned, favour compulsory training for the young lads and young men.
As I have, also, frequently pointed out, this training, even if war might never come, would 
be a great benefit to them from the manhood viewpoint. They would be better physically, mentally and morally. A higher standard of manhood -would be established for Peace, and in case War should ever come, the Nation would be ready to defend its loved ones and its honour.
Since the outbreak of the War, Canada has raised considerably more than four hundred thousand men for all military purposes. This is about one hundred thousand men for each million of British birth or descent. After deducting the number of enlisted soldiers of other than British birth or descent, this still shows a higher percentage of enlistment than has oc-cui red in Great Britain, or, I believe, any other country. This has been under the voluntary system.
But the War has assumed gigantic proportions beyond what was anticipated. It is no longer a War of peoples or nations, it is a War of the sacred principles of human liberty against Prussian autocracy and tyranny. It is a question of men and munitions. At last the munition problem is being fairly well met. The men problem is not yet solved. Sir William Robertson, Chief of the General Staff; Mr. Lloyd George, Secretary of State for War; Mr. Bonar Law, Colonial Secretary; Mr. Asquith, the Prime Minister, as well as His Majesty the King, have each and all pointed out that it is now a question of "men and. still more men."
There are parts of Canada which have not yet been successfully reached by voluntary enlistment. Whether or not the influences against voluntary enlistment are backed up by Prussian gold, is a question as yet not fully determined.
There are, in Canada, of all British origins, vide the last census returns, less than 3,900,000; there are of French origin upwards of 2,000,000 ; German origin about 400,000 ; of Austro-Hungarian origin about 130,000, etc., etc.
Britain at the outset of the war, resorted to voluntary enlistment only; but after having exhausted every available means that could be used under the voluntary system, the Nation, in the end, has had to resort to Compulsory service. On every hand, able-bodied "slackers" were seen. Families would send one, two three, and sometimes more, sons to the Front, while the neighbours would remain at home, filling the positions vacated by those gallant boys.
The same principle has been carried out in Canada, only on a broader scale. There may be some excuses for those of German and Austro-Hungarian descent hesitating to enlist ; there can be none for any other nationality. However, to their credit, a considerable number of gallant Canadians of these nationalities have enlisted and have done splendid service at the Front.
I have evidence in my possession, that there are distinct movements abroad, in parts of Canada, whereby persons are urged not to go to the Front; not to fight, but to let these of British descent go away and leave open their positions in order that those who remain as "slackers" should fill them.
Such condition is certainly unfair to the gallant fellows who have risked their lives in the service. In short, one might as well claim that the paying of taxes should be voluntary, as the defending the Empire, in such a crisis, should be voluntary.

Of course, proper exemption should be made for the maintenance of our great industrial, agricultural, commercial and other requirements at home; but this exemption can only be arrived at after complete inquiry and registration. .
I, therefor, have the honour, in view of all the circumstances, to recommend that the gravity of the situation, the justice of the cause, the preservation of the Liberties of our Canadian people and the successful issue of the War require a system of compulsory service, with careful observation of the above safeguards.
Will you kindly give this your best consideration andr should you agree with the principle involved, may I hope that effect will at an early date be given thereto.
Faithfully,
(Sgd) Sam Hughes.
The Right Honourable,
Sir Robert L. Borden, G.C.M.G.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
I received no answer to that proposition. It is also well known that prominent members of the Cabinet, up till a couple of weeks ago, declared that, there would be no compulsory service. It is further asserted that shortly before the Prime Minister sailed for England, definite pledges were given to certain dignitaries against conscription. In the presence of the Prime Minister during last December, the Chairman of the National Service Commission several times declared that compulsory service was out of the question; that to introduce it would mean civil war. The Minister of Militia, Hon. Sir Edward Kemp, quite recently declared in the House that the question of compulsory service had never been considered by the Cabinet. I have always pursued the educative line, realizing that men who are not informed on the subject tend to cater to fads and fancies of the public mind. They forget that under responsible government ministers must have the courage of their convictions-as was pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday, in theory-and be leaders of public opinion; that only under autocratic forms of Government should advisers of the Crown be influenced by agitations forced upon them, and that the duty of members of Parliament is to educate kindly. Therefore, have I pursued a moderate line.
Had my aim been personal advancement or influence, or my desire to injure or embarrass the Government, it would have been easy early in the session, when such a motion would not have been accepted, to force it on the House. But my ambition is solely to help the boys at the front to win the war; therefore I took no action until I
felt that the Cabinet and the country were well educated up to the line. Again, therefore, knowing the trend of a government to await being encouraged to act, have I pursued the educative policy, my aim being the success of my plans.
The day after the Prime Minister's return to Canada, with this same end in view, I sent him a letter. As it is not personal, I assume that there is no objection on the part of the Prime Minister to my reading it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.

It was as follows'
May 16, 1917.
Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden,
Prime Minister,
.	Ottawa.
Dear Sir Robert:
I have waited until your return before taking action in relation to our efforts in the war, or rather our lack of effort in the. war.
I have given notice of a motion on going into the Committee of Supply in favour of compulsory service. This is not intended to be a want of confidence motion, if you cart give me any assurance that the Government will seriously take up the question itself, and that energetic and effective action along right lines will follow.
X shall be glad if you will arrange a date this week, or early next, when this matter might he discussed in Parliament.
Faithfully,
(Sgd.) Sam HughtsH.
The Prime Minister responded in his speech on the following Friday, enunciating the principle of compulsory overseas service. I, therefore, heartily endorsed the proposition he then made, and have hoped that the details of the measure would be such as to receive general approval. I had one, and only one, aim in all this business: to win the war; let Canada and Canadians, each and all do our duty, our full duty; let us maintain our civilization; let us not weary in well-doing, but stand or fall by the boys in the trenches. To raise troops for compulsory overseas service was the watchword.
Let us put a few questions. First, has Canada the authority to put in force a measure of compulsory service? The right hon. leader of the Opposition says that Canada has not that authority, and on that point we! must cross swords with him. Second, what does that mean? Third, what does it involve? Fourth, what are the advantages? Fifth, what are the disadvantages or objections? Sixth, can it be accomplished, and with what consequences? Seventh, should there be exemptions? If so, of what nature? Eighth, how soon can it be ac-

complished? Ninth, will such soldiers be suitable? Tenth, why is a compulsory service necessary? Why not continue the voluntary system?
Let me refer to the first question: has Canada the authority? Section 15 of the British North America Act says:
The Commander in Chief of the Land and Naval Militia, and of all naval and military-forces, of and in Canada, is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the Queen.
" The Queen " here means, of course, the Governor General in Council. Section 91 of the British North America Act says:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this Act) the exclusive legislative authority of the Parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say,-
Sub-Sec. 7, Militia, Military and Naval Service and Defence.
That is all the British North America Act has bearing on the subject. The Militia Act goes further. The interpretation clause, section 2, says:
(b) 'Emergency', means war, invasion, riot or insurrection, real or apprehended.
(g) 'On active service,' as applied to a person subject to military service, means whenever he is enrolled, enlisted, drafted or warned for service or duty, during an emergency, or when he is on duty, or has been warned for duty in aid of the civil power.
Then section 4 deals with the command in chief.
Inasmuch, Mr. SpeakeT, as this legal aspect of the question was largely set forth in an address which I had the honour of delivering to the House in January, if it is permissible, I would like it to be taken as read.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Perhaps it would be better if the hon. gentleman proceeded in the usual way.

All right. Section 4 says:
The command in chief of the militia is declared to continue and be vested in the King, and shall be exercised and administered by His Majesty or by the Governor General as his representative.
" Governor-General " means, of course, the Governor-General in Council. Section 69, which deals with active service, provides:

The Governor in Council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
Section 72, which deals with command in time of war, is as follows:
In time of war, when the militia is called out for active service conjointly with His Majesty's regular forces, His Majesty may place in command thereof a senior general officer of his regular army.
That has been the case at the front; we have had a senior general officer in command of the Canadian Expeditionary Force.
Section 74 of the Militia Act (Army Act and Regulations) is our charter for our service beyond the seas, just as the British North America Act covers the administration of Canada. Section 74 reads:
The Army Act for the time being in force in the United Kingdom, the King's regulation, and all other laws applicable to His Majesty's troops in Canada and not inconsistent with this Act or the regulations made thereunder, shall have force and effect as if they had been enacted by the Parliament of Canada for the government of the militia.
I would like the right hon. leader of the Opposition to note this. Thus Canada has full authority at any time to enrol and train her militia. The Government, if they chose to do so, could, in time of peace or in time of war, call out 300,000 men and train them; they could do it to-morrow. Canada has authority to send them overseas, for the defence of Canada, in an emergency, and "war" is an emergency, according to the interpretation clause of the Act.
Canada" has full authority to equip, officer, and manage her forces as she pleases while they are within her borders. Beyond her borders and within her own laws, Canadian authority for management and control is wanting, except by adopting the Army Act. Canada has no constitutional authority, as I interpret it-and, of course, I am giving my own interpretation-to administer or control our men once we send them beyond our border until we adopt, as the law provides, the Army Act and the clauses relating thereto. After we have adopted the section of the Army Act in this regard, that section is as much a part of our constitution and law as is the British North America Act, and this Government and Parliament have as much authority to carry on the management of the militia under that law as if it were part and parcel of the British North America Act. But the British military law, especially the Army Act, gives that authority to Canada. The

statesmen and war officers of Great Britain have foreseen such situations as now present themselves. Not only in cases where the colonial Governments raise the troops and pay the cost, but even where Britain enrols and pays colonials, the British Government has by law safeguarded, in every conceivable instance, the rights, privileges and liberties of the colonials. Therefore the Canadian forces are in no sense "British regulars." I come now to a consideration of the British military law, 1914. I refer first to the Army Act, section 190, subsection 23, page 557, which says:
The expression "colony" means any part ol His Majesty's dominions exclusive of the British Islands and of British India, and includes Cyprus and any British protectorate, and where parts of such dominions are under both a central and a local legislature, all parts under the central legislature shall, for the purpose of this definition, be deemed to be one colony.
Chapter XI., page 194, military law, provides that the military forces of the Crown shall consist of three classes, British, Indian and Colonial. Colonial forces are defined by section 3 as follows:
The colonial forces are of two classes, namely, the forces raised by the government of a colony, and the forces raised in a colony by direct order of His Majesty to serve as auxiliary to, and in fact to form part for the time being of, the regular forces.
I should like the leader of the Opposition to take note of this, because later on I intend to point out a flaw in his argument. There are two classes of colonial forces. I have no record of the Canadian Government having sent a despatch to the British authorities asking that sections 175 and 176 of the Army Act be made applicable to Canada, but I presume they did so. There was no necessity, however, for doing that unless we desired to let the British authorities enrol troops in Canada and pay them. The Governor General in Council might pass a thousand Orders in Council in regard to those sections, but they would not be worth the paper they were written on, because sections 175 and 176 refer to other classes of colonial troops raised by the British Government with the consent of the colony and paid for by the British Government. They do not apply in any sense to the Canadian Expeditionary Force. I did not know that that action was taken until the leader of the Opposition so stated the other day, but that is why I have claimed from the outset that those troops were under the control of the Minister of Militia, that is, under the control of Canada, and should be controlled by Canada, because sections
175 and 176 deal with the class of colonial troops that are not referred to here. If the British authorities were to enlist men in Canada for aeroplane service or anything of that sort and pay them and control them, then they would come under sections 175 and 176, but not otherwise. Section 177 is the section which applies to us, and I will refer to it a little later on. Chapter 11 of the military law goes on to state:
The first class of colonial forces-those raised by the government of a colony-are only subject to the Army Act when so provided by the law of the colony and when serving with part of His Majesty's regular forces, and then only so far as the colonial law has not provided for their government and dicipline, and subject to the exceptions specified in the general orders of the general officer commanding the forces with which they are serving. The Army Act, however, section 177, provides that the colonial law may extend to the forces, although beyond the limits of the colony where they are raised.
The second class of colonial forces-of which the West India regiment, the Royal Malta Artillery, the West African Regiment, the non-Europeans of the Fortress Companies, Royal Engineers, at Hong Kong and Sierra Leone, and the Hong Kong Singapore Battalion, Royal Garrison Artillery, are examples-is referred to by sections 175, subsection 4, and 176, subsection 3, of the Army Act. Their pay and maintenance are voted annually by the Imperial Parliament, and they are in fact Imperial forces, although serving in a colony.
Section 177 is one which gives to Canada supreme control of her troops, not in Canada, as we have it here under the British North America Act, but in England and at the front. The Army Act, section 177, page 539, provides:
Where any force of volunteers, or of militia, or any other force, is raised in India or in a colony, any law of India or the colony may extend to the officers, non-commissioned officers and men belonging to such force, whether within or without the limits of India or the colony; and any such law may apply, in relation to sudh force and to any officers, non-commissioned officers and men thereof, all or any of the provisions of this Act, subject to such adaptations, modifications and exceptions as may be specified in such law, and where so applied this Act shall have effect in relation to such force, subject to such adaptations, modifications and exceptions as aforesaid; and where any such force is serving with part of His Majesty's regular forces, then so far as the law of India or the colony has not provided for the government and dicipline of such force, this Act and any other Act for the time being amending the same shall, subject to such exceptions and modifications as may be specified in the general orders of the general officer commanding His Majesty's forces with which such force is serving, apply to the officers, non-commissioned officers and men of such force, in like manner.
This section shall not apply to any officer belonging to any such force when attached to or doing duty with, or to any non-commissioned officer or man belonging to any sudh force when attached to or otherwise acting as part

of or with, any portion of the regular, reserve, or auxiliary forces in the United Kingdom.
That sub-section means this: Prior to 1914, we were in the habit of letting some of our forces go overseas for the purpose of taking part in tournaments, the Queen's Jubilee, etc. The leader of the Opposition will remember instances of that. Although our troops wore the British uniform, they were not under British military law, and they were not under the law of Canada, because until we adopted section 177, we had no control over them beyond the three-mile limit. The section was enacted so as to meet this difficulty, so that while those soldiers were in England, while no Canadian law would cover their case, they would be attached to the British command and would be subject to that command for the time being.
I hesitate to differ from the leader of the Opposition, but I respectfully take the ground that it is admitted that Canada has the right to call out the whole militia, or any part thereof, to-morrow, whether in times of peace or war, for training purposes. It is admitted that Canada has the right to train, officer and arm these troops for the defence of this country, whether within or without Canada; and if we send these troops one inch beyond the three-mile limit of Canada we might just as well send them 3,000 miles away to the German frontier, because Canada's defence is not restricted to one inch, or one mile, or one thousand miles distance'from her coasts, but is wherever Canada is threatened. I take the ground that we have the authority to do all these things within Canada, and in view of section 177 of the British Army Act, we have legal authority to control these men ourselves beyond the three-mile limit of Canada.
Secondly: What does compulsory service mean? It does not prevent the citizen who prefers to be recorded as a volunteer from enlisting as such. If he does not volunteer the Government .should select men on a basis fair to all. These men must be trained and some of them sent overseas, but Canada must control and pay them there as well as here.
Thirdly, it involves the responsibility to the Canadian people for every man and every dollar. We have the responsibility now, but responsibility without the power to control constitutes an intolerable condition. Canada has already lost much in this regard. Compulsory service gives us this power.

The advantages of compulsory service are:
(a)	Under the volunteer plan the basis is' enthusiasm, love of liberty, intense patriotism, the setting aside all else for the cause- home, loved ones, position, wealth, aye, even life itself-and all for his personal love of a principle. The volunteer offers all, risks all, sacrifices all.
(b)	Under compulsory service the State adjusts inequalities, and instead, for example, of taking .all the boys in a family, leaving the neighbour's boys all at home, as frequently occurs under the voluntary system, the duty of service is fairly and evenly distributed. Tens of thousands of good Canadian fellows, willing to serve, are still in mufti because they do not think it fair for them to go and leave at home neighbours just as eligible, secure in comfort and drawing high pay in various industrial pursuits. After the war the one might be penniless, without a position, possibly shot to pieces and unfit to earn a livelihood, while the other would live in comparative luxury and health, enjoying the liberties so dearly earned by the former. '
(c)	Every citizen owes duty to the State; he must pay taxes, must be personally responsible fpr a share in the administration of justice, etc. So also, in every land, each is liable for service for the defence of homes and loved ones and against a common enemy to mankind.
(d)	Compulsory service dpes not imply a vast standing army, as I regret to say a few labour leaders are endeavouring to make it appear, and I was going to add, a few labour leaders bearing all the earmarks of being in the pay of German agents in the United States. My system implies training from ten to sixteen years of age in schools; then occasional brushing up in after years. But Canada in this emergency has not the preliminary training done; so other conditions must be applied.
(e)	'Conscription as in- Germany takes from his home and business in the best two pr three years of his life, in peace times, every male citizen. The man becomes lost ini the machine; under the brutal German system he becomes mentally and morally debased.
Under my proposal for compulsory overseas service, the men would be called out, and after preliminary training would cross the peean. The drawbacks attending the German system would be avoided. No autocratic class would be created; each soldier would have before him, by merit and fitness, the possibility of rising to senior position. The training would benefit each for

peace after the war; and above all, Canada would do her duty to the gallant fellows in the trenches. I venture the assertion that after a few weeks' training, the proudest men in Canada would be these lads, and they would all regret not having joined three years ago. When the war is over each will return to his duty as citizen, proud to have helped to overthrow the greatest autocracy that ever 'blighted humanity
(f)	There are only two free governments upwards of a century old, namely, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the United States. Why? Rulers become autocratic, selfish, corrupt, sycophantic, mere creatures of corporations and of so-called democratic organizations -because the greatest tyrant and autocrat is the so-called democrat, irresponsible to the whole people. It has been asserted that people's representatives in national assemblies too often become mere pawns on the checker-board. Even in Canada men are found who suggest-nay, who go farther and assert that two great corporations-one railway, and the other a financial group- control this Government and the business and administrative ends thereof. I am not endorsing this assertion, but merely giving vent to the rumour.

Simply putting it on
Hansard.

For ordinary wars
the voluntary system would usually more than suffice. This war, however, staggers humanity. It is beyond all former. comprehension; it is the bitter, tenacious, desperate struggle of dark-age autocracy against free democracy. For thirty years the autocratic German machine has been planning, getting ready, While the free democracies of France, of Britain, of Italy, and now of Russia and the United States, have been living in a fool's paradise, unprepared. Free democracies, properly trained and directed, will ever defeat autocracies. A good illustration of that is found in the old athletic days, when the amateur team always proved superior to the professional whether at lacrosse or football. _ The same is true in every land and under any circumstances, but the men must be trained. It is difficult, however, even in tree Canada to instil the idea that discipline is not repression; is not the breaking down of one's will; is not the restrictive limiting principles, 'but is the upbuilding, the educative, the 'strengthening, the controlling, the developing, the
training to control and to command idea. Canadians at the front have been so trained; hence the free, self-reliant Canadian citizen soldier has come out triumphant, although more or less weighted down by the machine idea and incubus of regular service systems.
What are the disadvantages worthy of note in a proper compulsory service system? I look at this thing from one end to the other and frankly I must confess that I do not find any, except such as are created by agitators for a special purpose, and these agitators will soon disappear for the people will not tolerate them.
Can compulsory service be accomplished? The right hon. leader of the Opposition says that it cannot. I again show my faith in the Canadians and cross swords with him.
I have every faith that it can he accomplished, and accomplished just as easily as rolling off a log, as the Yankee says. If taken up in the correct way the plan will he generally acceptable. It would be well of course that the public should be fully instructed in a kindly way as to their duty to serve in defence of homes, loved ones, free institutions and liberty. It might also be impressed upon some, a very limited few, that this is:
No time for wile or long intrigue,
Our country to her children cries,
Those who're not for us are against;
Better as foes than false allies.
According to Canada's census in 1911 there were in this country 1,700,000 males from 18 to 45 years. The immigration from 1911 to 1916 of persons from 18 to 45 years of age was 500,000. That is only an estimate but it is an estimate based on all the information at my disposal, because, out of the nearly 1,700,000 people who came to Canada during the years since the last census, of 1911, up to the present time, I estimate that 500,000 would be of the fighting age between 18 and 45. Then I accept about
100,000	less than the estimate of the statistician who prepared these figures as to the natural increase. I have put the amount of the average natural increase in population at 200,000 although, if I heard the figures correctly in. th,e House yesterday, it was put at over 300,000. The result is that Canada to-day has 2,420,000 fighting men between 18 and 45 years of age within her borders and at the front.
We have enrolled 420,000 men, which leaves two millions of men between the ages of 18 and 45 free for service. Of these two million men, 1,200,000 are single. I do not know how these figures compare with

those which were furnished yesterday, but, at all events, such is my estimate.
Of course, there will be certain exemptions and exceptions, but Canada could send another 200,000 men to the front and yet not weaken to any perceptible extent her producing capacity.
Should there be exemptions? I do not propose to enter into the details of the Bill to-day. My desire is that the Bill should go through with as little delay as possible and without any more discussion than is consistent with the proper consideration of the measure. But the exemptions would need to be very carefully looked at, and if I might here interject an idea, it is that one of the great objections to the conserip-tive Bill is the form of the tribunal that is to administer it, but that is a matter the Prime Minister said could be amended. There should be exemptions. The Militia Act provides for them and this Act also provides for them.
The next question is: How soon can the force be enrolled? I am not trying to bring in Valcartier at all, but I believe that an ordinary man capable of taking hold of this matter could have this force ready to go overseas within the next four months. Within the next four months Canada should raise, equip and train 150,000 men, and hy October they should be in the trenches. I do not think it would be much of a trick at all.
Will such soldiers be suitable? We have heard a good deal about boys not being fit to fight and not fit to do this and that. I have always had great faith in the boy. I was a boy once myself-you may not believe it, but it is true^and I still like to keep the boyish confidence. The most notable examples of bravery in this war have been afforded by lads mostly undsr 18 years of age. Thousands and tens of thousands of British, Canadian and Australian boys have displayed marvellous heroism and bravery. They fear nothing; they are ready to do anything. Then, to the question:	Will such soldiers Ibe suitable?-I say most assuredly, providing they are trained as citizen soldiers, and not repressed and dwarfed by permanent corps or regular service training. Discipline must not be regarded as repression but as development, education, polish, fitness. Train the boy to be self-reliant and fearless rather than to be an abject sort of machine.
It is sometimes supposed that young men do not make good soldiers. Let me once more impress upon the House that it was

the boys of the Welsh regiment who smashed the famous French cuirassiers at Quatre Bras. The average age of the battalion, old and young, was below 20. Upwards of thirty per cent of Wellington's heroes at Waterloo were under 20 years of age. Twenty-five per cent of the warriors who climbed the heights of Alma, and fought in that misty morn at Inkerman, were also under 20 years of age, many of them under 17, and they were dandies. They were trained to fight in those days with cudgels. In this present great war, many of the most heroic acts have been performed by mere lads of 18. There is no fear but such soldiers will be suitable in every (respect.
Why is compulsory service necessary? Compulsory service is necessary because the voluntary system, after accomplishing almost marvels, is exhausted. I have no exact evidence of it, but there is the best of reasons for believing that German gold, cleverly applied, did the trick. I do not for one moment believe that Bryan was bought by German gold in the United States but he was influenced by men who were bought by German gold. Henry Ford was approached by gentlemen who have since admitted, and sworn to it, that they were in the pay of the German agents who were influencing these gentlemen to take the line they did. I presume that if the evidence could all be brought out here, we would have some very interesting stories. I repeat that German gold, cleverly applied, did the trick. The records of American courts show clearly that the labour agitations, the contraband demands, the food riot movements, the "peace at any price" agitations, have all been controlled and directed by German gold. We have instances where gentlemen occupying high journalistic positions in this country were in receipt of money from the United States of America and it is now known, and it has been proved in the United States courts, that peace organizations in that country were to a very large extent maintained by German gold for years before the war. Early in 1916, when Canadian recruiting was at its zenith, whispers were heard from all Canadian centres-the work was skilfully done-dreading that workmen could not be found for the various industries and services in Canada. This matter was up in the House once before. I must here say in justice to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) that it had been intimated to me last night that he had stated that I had been a party to helping the munition workers to smuggle men out

for munition work instead of sending them to the front. I never did anything of the kind. The Prime Minister referred to this matter some time ago in the House and there is no harm in referring to it again.
I merely read extracts from Hansard and I had nothing whatever to say on the point myself.
I thought that the hon. gentleman made a comment coupling me with the Prime Minister in stating the claims of the munition workers.
I merely read what the minister said.

I will deal with that matter a little later. The dread was expressed that workmen could not be found for the various industries and services in Canada and it gradually took head. At the time I suspected German gold, and so informed the Prime Minister. The movement grew in force, and the Imperial Munitions Board, and the Finance Minister, each became anxious and restrictive. Finally the head of the Canadian Pacific Railway was influenced by the agitation, and while the Imperial Munitions Board and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance had limited themselves to impressive personal conversations with the Prime Minister and many others, Lord Shaughnessy went farther, and not only privately, as did the others, but openly, proclaimed himself in an address before the Board of Trade of Montreal. Lord Shaughnessy had been regarded in railway circles as a man of sound judgment; he had been trained under the greatest railway man of the age, Sir William van Horne; but he had not the breadth of judgment, had not the force of character, had not the fearlessness in face of trial of the great master, Van Horne.
He was not affected by German gold?
One would imagine from the wishy-washy criticism of the financial critic of the Opposition that there was some influence at him.
Oh, oh.

Whether that was a pat on the back or not I do not know. At this juncture I should point out that these agitations manifested themselves all over the country. The Prime Minister was bombarded with them. He was an easier mark than I. I would throw them out of my office. I
might recite this incident; the Prime Minister will not object. A very distinguished gentleman, head of one of the largest organizations in Canada, the manager of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company of Sydney, came to the oflice and, with tears in his voice and some in his eyes, begged us not to enlist and take the men away. I had chanced to visit that institution many years ago, and as I then went along the lines of furnaces and down through the coal mines,
I saw as handsome a lot of fellows as ever stood inside jackets, Highland Scotchmen every man of them. I had gone through it in after years and found hundreds of men not one of whom could speak the English tongue, and almost every one of them an alien enemy, in time of war. I asked the manager, as the Prime Minister may remember, what had become of these gallant fellows that he was now asking us to restrain from enlisting, in order that they might shovel coal and handle furnaces in Sydney. I pointed out that his foresight should have been exercised years back in keeping gallant Canadians of British descent in our country, in place of driving them out to the four winds of Heaven and filling their places with aliens from the mines of Germany and Austria.
The ex-Minister directed in writing that a young man in the city of Halifax be not permitted to enlist for service.

The gentleman has wakened up; I am glad to see it; I was not aware that he had enough vitality. The young man to whom he refers, I understood, had been a soldier, and as long as I was Minister of Militia or acting in any military capacity and a soldier undertook to act as that gentleman did, he would not be allowed to remain in the 4 p.m. service. But I learned afterwards that he was not a soldier at the time he had written the articles referred to, and accordingly I observed the law and I think I made him an officer. I know I gave him a chance anyway.

You prevented
him from enlisting.
I did not. He was dismissed from the forces, that was the order I gave.	'
You gave directions that he be not enlisted.
No, I gave directions that he be not appointed an officer.
The ex-Minister directed the officer commanding at Halifax that a certain individual there be not permitted to enlist as a private.

I do not remember the details. I do remember that this man had gone to the Old Country and had there written some of the most slanderous falsehoods; and I gave an order that if he was a soldier or an officer at the time, he should not be permitted to enter the forces of Canada, at all events until we had reason to believe he had learned his proper functions.
This agitation went on, then, about the labour question, and would you believe it, this man, the man who was in here demanding, with tears in his eyes, that we do not take the soldiers from Sydney, inside of two months was after me to give him command of a 'battery himself, and to take these very fellows away. The whole thing has been piffle from one end of Canada to the other. The Prime Minister, however, yielding to these influences-and I admit they were very serious, I was pestered with them until I threw them out-suggested to me a letting up in the recruiting. It was in vain that I protested and met the fallacious arguments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On what occasion was it that I suggested letting up on re-.cruiting?

The leader of the Government on more than one occasion-take the very day when Mr. McDougall was present, the leader of the Government asked me again if I could not lot up on recruiting; and, moreover, the right hon. leader of the Government later on pointed out-if he wants the whole story I will be glad to give it-pointed out that there was a tremendous agitation in Toronto over the subject, that he had had various communications from Toronto, that the Finance Minister had told him there was a perfect storm brewing there, and that agitation was due to the fact that men could not be obtained as workers. Mark Irish, of the Imperial Munitions Board; Mr. Flavelle, of the Imperial Munitions Board, and others had been insistent in their demands that these men would not be taken. If the Prime Minister will permit me, I will read letters that will cover the thing, letters from himself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would be very glad.

I would like the
Prime Minister to see one of the letters before I read it.
As a matter of fact, was not recruiting called off at Sydney and Glace Bay over a year ago?
I did not call it off. I will show the Prime Minister a copy of the letter; I have not the original here.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman can go on with his speech; I will make my reply.

Before I sailed for England in March, 1916, knowing that the Prime Minister had communicated his fears re the labour situation and the Quebec question to others-I might mention to Mr. Godfrey, of Toronto, and a number of others- and it being the transition period between winter billeting and spring encampment, I yielded to his request and partially let up o<n recruiting. I told the Prime Minister that the only excuse I could make was that it was between winter billeting and spring encampments at the time, and the records will show that we did not draw a man out, we did not give any men to the munitions; our officers simply did not exert themselves as vigorously as formerly, owing to the fact that we had no place to put the men without going to great expense, and spring camp6 were being formed.
It may he noted, incidentally, that these same organizations and gentlemen with affiliated interests, while prominent in patriotic and philanthropic professions, have, nevertheless, not been unmindful of the profiteering aspect o.f the war, hence, probably, their intense' interest in the labour question. Only this week the' head of the Munitions Board has taken it on himself to write a letter to the manufacturers of this country practically demanding that recruiting shall not interfere with his munitions, when every day if I go to. any big factory in Montreal or Toronto I can see hundreds of men clamouring for work. I have seen five hundred men around the entrance to a factory in Montreal in the morning looking for work, at the very time these gentlemen were saying that we were taking away their workmen. There are
10,000	women in Toronto to-day, and hundreds of men, anxious for work in munition factories, and yet these gentlemen tell the public and the Government that we are interfering with the work of the factories, when it is perfect nonsense to say 60.

Other contributing causes in the failing off of recruiting are, the abusive tone and language of many speakers at publio meetings, calling indiscriminately all those not enlisting "slackers," "cowards," "shirkers," and thus forcing honest men to get their backs against the wall and become negative instead of positive.

Speaking at Lindsay, Ontario, on April 28, regarding the conditions of which he spoke and the agitation, the hon. gentleman said:
This unfortunately had an effect upon the Prime Minister. The result was that I was asked in March, 1916, not to press recruiting, and recruiting to-day has been dead in Canada for fighting purposes.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say that the statement made by him in Lindsay is quite correct?

I am quite surprised at the hon. gentleman asking any such question. That speech is issued by myself, and I am not in the habit of issuing statements that I do not endorse. I will prove it before I have finished.
I had just referred to the abusive tone and language of many speakers at public meetings as one of the contributing causes in the falling off of recruiting. Many of these speakers were well-meaning gentlemen, fellows with their hair parted in the middle, coming out of the cities and towns, many of them not over the fighting age themselves, men who should have been in the trenches; and these men would lecture the fellows in the country. It is a pleasant task for city chaps to lecture country boys on their duty. I could mention fifty men from different places, all of fighting age, who had the hardihood to go out and lecture men who, from one cause or another, were not going to the front.
I may say that thus far-and I have had a good deal to do with it-whilst I have encouraged recruiting in every legitimate way by enthusiasm, along patriotic lines, I have never asked a man to go to the front. I have no right to do so. The actual action of certain prominent people in directing men not to go, but to stay at home, and secure the places of those going to the front, unfortunately has had its effect. Since the ex-Prime Minister, the hon. leader of the Opposition, is so wedded to his beloved province Quebec, I regret to say that that is a charge which he might well inquire into, relating to the common clergy of his own province.
The removal from Ontario, or rather the establishment of industries in Quebec province, because, as the excuse was, "labour is scarce in Ontario, so many having gone to the war; but plentiful in Quebec, whence few have enlisted"-this regard I took up the question, upon representation from Col. Thomas A. Duff, with Sir Joseph Flavelle, and Sir Robert Borden, with the result that these industries are now more fairly distributed, and the British provinces are not so much penalized because of their enlistment.
I thought it well to present to the House a memo on that subject. A very large industry is being erected at Maisonneuve, and the reason given by those who are establishing it was that they could not get labour in Toronto, so many men had gone to the front, but they could get plenty in Montreal because none had gone. This came to Colonel Duff's attention, and he sent me the correspondence, which T forwarded to Sir Robert, and I think action has been taken on it. The following is the letter which I sent to Mr. Flavelle:
October 30, 1916.
Dear Mr. Flavelle,-
From Colonel Thomas A. Duff of Toronto, one of the most worthy and reputable citizens of Ontario, the following letter has been received :
"3 Maynard Ave., Toronto.
October 26th, 1916.
"Dear Sir Sam,-
"In the belief that you are not aware of the action outlined herein, I desire to present to your notice, the following:
"Recently, it is understood, the Imperial Munitions Board, under the leadership of Mr. J. W. Flavelle, of Toronto, and Mr. Gordon, of Montreal, has let a contract with an American firm for munitions, involving the erection of a plant for the manufacture of fuses in Canada. These commodities are, of course, for the British Government, and the contract is let by that Government through the Imperial Munitions Board in Canada.
"I understand that the Board expressed the desire that the work should be done remote from the Atlantic seaboard-at Toronto or other suitable interior centre. It is further reported that this American firm declined to go to Toronto, or in Ontario, because it was said workmen could not he obtained, so many men having gone as soldiers to the war.
"Rumor has it that this great industry will, therefore, he located by the Imperial Munitions Board in, or adjoining, the city of Montreal, where labour is plentiful.
"Now, sir, how does this matter stand? Wise military precautions require such industries to he removed from the seaboard.
"The excuse is put forward that labour cannot be obtained in Toronto. Why, sir, this is absurd. Toronto has many returned soldiers who have manfully done their duty for King, country and liberty, and who are competent for such work. There are many
The hon. gentleman has not mentioned the 49th and 51st Battalions.

These battalions, which were raised long before that, were not mentioned by the member for Edmonton. I am merely quoting the statement of the member for Edmonton r.nd dealing with the battalions that he mentioned as having been recruited in Edmonton at the same time.
There has been a lot of guff, privately and publicly, along this line. I remember that the Minister of Finance on one occasion became excited over the raising of three battalions in Toronto. If the Prime Minister does not object, I purpose reading some letters dealing with these battalions. There is one here which is marked "confidential"; I will let the Prime Minister see it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not care to examine letters in the House. If my hon. friend desires to read confidential letters, one would suppose that the proper course would be to show them to one in advance. The hon. gentleman will have to take his own course in the matter.

Well, I am prepared to take my own course in the matter; I shall not read the letter. It has been referred to in the House, however. There is nothing in my letter that I am ashamed of, and it also is marked confidential. However, if the Prime Minister does not wish the letter to be read-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was it a letter written to me?
It was written by the Prime Minister to me.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As to reading it, my hon. friend will have to take his own course.
Certainly I will take my own course; I will not read it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the date of it?

This does not imply that we would string all our men out in one long firing line. We might hold no more of a front than we now do but we should have behind these trenches battalions, brigades, divisions and even corps, taking their turn in the trenches to get trained. Then, should exhaustion take place, it would be time enough to amalgamate a little at a time until elimination would occur, and until victory or defeat would be ours. We would then have our men practically experienced and the original intention in raising the soldiers would he carried out. So far as recruiting for the future in Canada is concerned, your promise of half a million men could easily be fulfilled. But it will not be fulfilled if you permit yourself to be hampered by raising little drafts here and little drafts there sent over in charge of junior lieutenants.
This work is carried on by inspiration, not by fatheads, muddleheads or woodenheads. There has been a clean-cut system from the beginning. Every possible effort has been made in certain quarters to interfere with the force and keep it down to serfdom, to mistrust it and to humiliate it. That sort of thing must cease.
Bonaparte, as well as every other soldier of genius, recognized that dividing the soldiers' maximum efficiency into four parts, only one part depended on the actual man. Pride in himself, faith and confidence in his cause, belief in his leaders, etc., constituted the other three. Bonaparte had no use for wooden-heads. He always claimed that-give him French officers, with a mixture of British soldiers, not English alone, but British, and these included large forces of Scotch, Irish and Welsh, in his wars-he would trim the World.
The Prime Minister stated that he thought if I wanted to read a letter, I should have consulted him first. Last October I sent him a letter in regard to compulsory service, but he never took the trouble to reply. Early in May I had a notice of motion before the House, but the Prime Minister did not pay any attention to it. I think, therefore, that I need not go out of my way to consult him in regard to reading letters in the House. I am ready to say on the floor of the House anything that I have to say, and as soon as the Prime Minister treats me in a courteous manner, I will act in the same way towards him.
History records that free governments, that is, responsible governments, gradually yield to petty bickerings; these to uncontrolled dogmatism; that to autocracy, and to dissolution. Nations and peoples forget that " Eternal vigilance is the price of liberty."
It has frequently been asserted that a responsible government is unfit to manage a nation in time of war, and that it should then give place to a dictatorship, or an autocracy. I have never believed in any such doctrine, and I hesitate not to affirm
ISir Sam Hughes.]
that no condition of affairs can arise which cannot be met efficiently under proper responsible government. The bases of popular government are intelligent, independent, interested, free men and women; Canada has these in millions. Secondly, the jealous guarding of the rights, first of ourselves, and then of others; this is not always properly observed in Canada, I regret to say. Thirdly, popular government demands equal rights and equal laws for all, and special privileges for none; this is not observed in Canada. Lastly it demands loyal, unselfish level-headed statesmen, who will not be misled by personal ambition or any other improper influence; Canada is not altogether deficient in this respect.
In either war or peace, the Cabinet should be properly controlled. No 'Government could possibly last under a system where each minister would be privileged to dabble and meddle in the details, not only of his own department, but of every other one. The Prime Minister should be familiar with all matters, except routine, being informed by the minister of the particular department; but only great questions of policy should concern the other departments. Non-observance of this principle, owing to the fact that following the Canadian Cabinet rule for generations, no minister has the right to manage his own department, but is subject to meddling, hindrance, and interferences from all other minsters' besides the Prime Minister, has primarily caused the failure of the volutary system of enlistment.
Oh.

It is the same with every Government. There is not an hon. gentleman opposite who managed his own department when he was minister. We have the evidence of one man that they " fought like blazes." It is a Prime Minister's right, and his only, to be satisfied by the minister of a department on matters other than that of policy.
It may not be amiss here once more to review voluntary enlistment. For the First Division my action was unique in history. All red tape was thrown aside and paternalism, which is one of the many banes of regular service systems, was entirely removed. Canada's citizen soldiers, not only then, but since, manfully proved my faith in them. In my absence in England, the debilitating plan of draft was resorted to, but I cancelled it on my return.

For the Second Division, during the winter months and at leisure, battalions were organized in various centres.
During 1915, it became evident, the war was more serious than anticipated', and that more men were needed. I resorted for the fall and winter of 1915-16 to the Home Locality System of recruiting. Nothing in history ever surpassed its success. I had plans laid for four hundred thousand men. Meantime the Prime Minister pledged five hundred thousand men. Personally, I have never seen why any limit should be fixed. We are in the war to establish human liberty and overthrow Kaiserism; and if it takes a million men for Canada's share they certainly should he sent. To complete the balance, however, of the five hundred thousand, the country was informally divided off so as to give, in general terms, about twice the area assigned for a battalion in the Home-Locality System. In short, for the Home-Locality System, a district of about forty thousand population was allotted to a battalion. In the last plan the unit was increased to about one hundred thousand This would have given between 525,000 and
550,000	men. During the winter of 1915-16, however, petty interferences began to hinder the work. These continued on into 1916, till finally, no battalion could be organized without delays. For example, before I left for England last June, I ordered the formation of three battalions in Manitoba. On my return in October they had not yet run the gauntlet of the Treasury Board and Privy Council. The three battalions have never yet been properly completed. Under my system they would have been ready to sail for England by the time they were finally authorized. However, I raised upwards of four hundred thousand men directly and indirectly with very little friction, and with the most marvellous good conduct and efficiency on the part of the soldiers.
Then, however, came the action early in 1916 regarding the labour question, and that was the beginning of the end of voluntary recruiting.
More than a month has elapsed since the Prime Minister's return, and his announcement of " Selective Conscription ". The Militia Act, which, according to the Prime Minister has all the powers of this Bill except " selection ",-or, to use his own words, " Thus, the pnly new feature proposed is the method of selection " to my mind is far more easy of application, broader and better adapted to the situation
than this Bill. I do not favour selection by tribunals under the Justice Department;
I prefer the ballot under the Militia Department. Under either plan troops will be allotted to a score of different departments in the actual militia service. Under the Bill they cannot be allotted to other employment. The Prime Minister read a list the other day of fprty different branches of employment to which men could be allotted under the Bill. Under the Militia Act, however, men could be allotted to any national service, such as farmers, mechanics, miners, business men, etc. All would receive military, uniform rates of pay. Under this Bill, however, the man at home nightly in a feather bed may receive from $7 to $10 as a mechanic, while his brother in the trenches receives $1.10 for hard work and being shot at. Under the Militia Act the men could be now undergoing training in Canada, for I have yet to learn of the man objecting to training our men to defend homes, principles and loved ones.
Meantime, therefore, while the next few months are being wasted in discussion of this Bill-in appointing the machinery to carry out its measures, in hearing the tedious judicial appeals, in organizing the training camps, and in conducting the elections 

let Canada act as she can act under the existing Militia Act until this Bill becomes law. There need be no delay, np friction, no need of compulsion to go overseas. The only compulsion would be to train, and no one cpuld object to. that. The machinery is ready. If the 'Government are actuated by honest desire to help on the cause they deserve credit. But I pass by every objection; set aside esveTy obstacle; blot out every adverse claim; refuse to heed any criticism against the principles of the Bill. 1 stand for the Bill, and will help to make it a success-if such is possible. I wish tp give it every chance; improve it, without loss of time; get it into operation forthwith, so that our beloved boys at the front may be properly suppprted, and the great cause of human liberty may be triumphant.
Let me appeal to the veteran leader of the Opposition to join, after pointing out his objections to the Bill, in having it become effective; grant a year's extension pf Parliament, and have action such that our land under this Act may be in the firing line by the end of September.
I turn for a moment to some of the remarks made by the leader of the Opposition yesterday. He suggested that the Gov-
Perhaps the ex-minister might tell us how many Boss rifles are now in use by the Canadian forces at the front?

I do not think there are any; I am not sure about that. All I know is that the Boss rifle is 'better than -the Lee-Enfield, but when the Prime Minister spoke to me about withdrawing it I knew the agitation that had gone on and which had been promoted by men who did not know that it was the ammunition that was the cause of the jamming. Although I know this quite well, I did not want to send soldiers . into the trenches, who, by reason of this agitation, might not have confidence in the rifle. Therefore, inasmuch as the agitation had caused a want of confidence on the part of some of the boys, and in the interest of all parties concerned, I thought it would be well not to have a fight during the progress of the war over the matter, but to withdraw the rifle and allow it to be used for training purposes.
Who started the agitation?
Would the ex-minister say what was the number of casualties amongst the Canadians in the battle of Zillebeke? [DOT]

The number is available but surely the hon. gentleman knows that the battle of Zillebeke was a shell fight. Our fellows were pounded by shells and there was not a rifle shot fired at them. It was long range fire and shells by the hundred were rained on them, the trenches were flattened out-I was there and saw the

place-it was worse than any ploughed field, and the boys went down. Harry Baker's battalion was there, it was long range fire and high explosive shells were sent over.

The question of the efficiency of the Ross rifle is a serious question to the people of Canada. I have asked the minister how many Canadians lost their lives in the battle of Zillebeke. The Canadians were armed with Ross rifles on that occasion and General Sir Douglas Haig reports that in that battle the Ross rifle jammed in the hands of the Canadians.

The Canadians were not armed with the Ross rifle at the battle of Zillebeke last June. The third division never were armed with the Ross rifle there. I do not know that there were any Ross rifles at the battle of Zillebeke. I have great respect for Sir Douglas Haig, but it would not matter one particle to me, knowing the facts, if all the reports in the universe said to the contrary. The hon. gentleman is altogether wide in his remarks. The first division that had been armed with the Lee-Enfield rifle for months found that the rifle jammed just the same as the other did but the cause was bad ammunition.

The hon. gentleman
spoke of an agitation against the Ross rifle. Who started the agitation against the Ross rifle?

The hon. member looks for information. I refer him to the pages of Hansard long years ago to gratify his thirst for knowledge. He knows as well as I know, and I am not going to take up time or dig up "dead corpses" here to-day. Let the hon. gentleman rest patient. He looks innocent, but he is anything but innocent.
Mr. Speaker, we are at war. Our boys have done magnificent work at the front, second to no troops in the world-I will not say better, but second to no troops in the world. They are suffering heavy losses. The Prime Minister has been at the front. I waited for his return. I knew he would be impressed by what he saw there. What may have been his views in the past on compulsory service, I know not and care not, but to-day he has brought down his Bill and is going in for compulsory service. I do not like the term conscriptive selection; but a rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and that is a matter of detail. I do not like the form of the measure; I should have preferred the Militia Act, which, I think, would have worked more

smoothly and been quicker in its operation. There is scarcely anything, if there is anything at all, in this Bill that could not have been carried out under the Militia Act. It must be remembered that we would not be called on to ballot for every soldier under the Militia Act. It would be possible to pass an Order in Council under the War Measures Act and so to call
5 p.m. out any class. But, in any event, we can call the militia out for training under the Militia Act, even if we do not send them overseas, and, in the name of Heaven, while this discussion is going on in the House, and if there is to be fighting while we are making our explanations here, let the boys be called out in the meantime and be trained under the Militia Act. That can be done and no one can object to it, and then when the Bill passes in some proper form we can apply its provisions and send them overseas if they do not volunteer. But I have faith that the boys called out for training would nearly all volunteer for service overseas. I will not throw a single impediment, directly or indirectly, in the way of the passing of this Bill, but will help on in every proper manner its passage through the House, in order that the boys at the front may be fully and properly protected and supported in their great struggle.

Mr. Speaker, coming to a conclusion in my own mind in regard to the Military Service Bill now under discussion in this House on motion for second reading, I regret to say that, in regard to the principle of the Bill, I find myself in rather serious conflict with the opinions of my leader, and I think also with the opinions of the large majority of my political friends sittting upon this side of the House. Under ordinary circumstances I would feel very deep regret, very sincere concern, if that were the case, and had it not been for the kindly, generous and patriotic words of counsel and advice which my honoured leader has addressed not only to me but to all his followers with regard to this measure, I might feel some embarrassment, and not a little unpleasantness. His words of advice to the whole of us were that in regard to this measure he himself would prefer that each member should be guided solely by the dictates of his own conscience, entirely without regard to the ordinary and well recognized ties of party. For this reason I feel the more free to express without any reservation my own views and conclusions in regard to the

measure, dictated alike by my conscience, my heart and my judgment. And, after having given to the Bill the best consideration it is in my power to bestow upon it, I find that I cannot agree in the conclusions so ably expressed, so forcibly uttered, by my honoured leader in the House yesterday.
One is, I think, bound to consider every sentence, every word uttered by the right hon. leader of the Opposition in regard to this matter. We know that his learning on the subject is most profound, we know that his parliamentary experience is not only the longest, but I think undoubtedly the most brilliant, in the annals of this Canadian Parliament. But, notwithstanding these things, acting upon my own judgment, judging the measure as well as I can, I have come to the conclusion that my support should go to this Bill and that it should be a whole-hearted support. In my opinion, the principle involved in the Military Service Bill at this very moment is one to the advantage of the people of Canada, to the advantage of Canada herself, to the advantage of the Empire and to the advantage of our Allies. For these reasons I intend to support it. While I make that general statement in regard to my support of the Bill, I still leave myself free in regard to criticise some of its details. I think that in many respects the Bill may yet be usefully amended, and if I correctly understood -the Prime Minister when he introduced the Bill into this House, and also when he spoke on the second reading of the Bill yesterday, he expressed a sincere desire on behalf of himself and of his Government, that he should receive any serious and useful suggestions by way Of amendment to the Bill-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-in order that the proposal, so far as possible, may in its operations be rendered absolutely free from partisanship, political prejudice, bias, or other baneful influence. And when the proper time comes I think I may be able to make some suggestions which will not operate as voiding the principle of the Bill, but will, I think, smooth its operations, and will perhaps place it in greater favour with the public at large.
There is just one observation I might make here, and that is that I have one other reservation to make, and to my mind it is a very important one; that is with reference to the question of conscription in general. I cannot bring myself to believe that this Bill is the full Government
policy in regard to the question of conscription. I cannot bring myself to believe that this is the last word on conscription in the proper sense of the word that we are to have from the Government during the present session of the present Parliament. Conscription, to my mind, involves the taking of more than manhood, more than flesh and blood.
I wpuld vote to withhold the operation of this Bill unless the Government is prepared to go further, and, during the present session, bring in concurrent legislation which would operate as a conscriptive measure upon the wealth and resources of Canada in general for the purposes of this war. This is a matter which, I think, touches my heart almost as much as any phase of the war. I do not like to feel that we, in this Parliament, think lightly of the flesh and .blood of the people of Canada, and think highly of the accumulated wealth of, the country, and that we will touch the one and dare not touch the other. May it never be said in Canada, or of Canada, in the words of the late Thomas Hood, the English poet: " Oh God, that wealth should be so dear, And flesh and blood so cheap."
I believe the people of Canada, when they speak of conscription in the meetings which have been held, where they have applauded the doctrine of conscription, meant something different from the conscription provided in this Bill. I believe, in the minds of the people, conscription of wealth, conscription of industry, and of resources, are included, and I trust that, during the present session, the Government will take steps to bring in concurrent legislation, more appropriately, no doubt, embodied in another Bill, which will let the people see that flesh and blood are noit lightly held, and that wealth is not lightly exempt. I can place before myself the picture that any hon. member in this House can conjure up, if he so desires, of the man over military .age, snugly settled in his own household, checking up his profit ledger, his stocks, bonds, debentures, mortgages and other investments, knowing that he has nothing very much at stake in the war at the present time, agreeing readily that the youth of Canada shall go to the front, and shall fight our battles, and that, so far, he has been practically exempt from any burdens of the war.
Hear, hear.

Some of those men live more cheaply than the ordinary middle class man. They are not taxed more than

the other man is under the tariff. They pay nothing directly into the treasury of the Government for the purposes of the war. This is a thing I would like to see remedied.
I believe the people of Canada would be willing to be placed-nay, desire to be placed-upon an equal footing with the people of Great Britain, with regard to this war, and I, for one, cannot understand why so able a man as the Minister of Finance of Canada has, from year to year, postponed this question of taxing wealth. He has taxed the industries. He has clipped the manufacturers' profits, rightly or wrongly. He has taxed munition profits, and I believe they can bear more taxation. Why he cannot adopt that system of righteousness and equality in regard to the income of the rich man, I cannot understand. The Minister of Finance is a strong, man. He understands the situation in Canada, and knows the public feeling. If he were given a free hand, he might act, but there must be some withholding force on the action of the Minister of Finance in regard to this matter. What that force is, I do not know, but people will conjure up certain things in their minds, when they get no explanation, because, at the opening of the war session in August, 1914, the matter was mentioned; and in the sessions of 1915 and 1916, and again this year, the matter has been brought most pointedly to the attention of the Minister of Finance. Each time he has put it off. He has procrastinated, and given reasons, which satisfy him, apparently, why the wealth of the country should not be taxed, but the time is coming when the people will imagine certain influences are behind the minister, unless he takes action. I trust that he will do so this session. If the Government will combine the conscription of wealth and resources of the country with the conscription of men for the firing line, I believe they will be backed, almost from one end of the Dominion of Canada to the other.
Having wandered, perhaps, a little from the Bill immediately before us, I will make a very brief survey of the position of Canada in reference to the war, from its outbreak in August, 1914, to the present time. I desire to make a consecutive statement, in order that the voters, whom I have the honour to represent in Parliament, may know my reasons for supporting this Bill, which emanates from the Government side, as it has not been very much my custom to support Government measures in the past seven years.

Most happily, Canada's experiences of war have been of very modest proportion and at long intervals, until the fata] day in August, 1914. War in 1914 found Canada and all or many of the present allied countries in a comparative state of unpreparedness, or perhaps, I would be speaking more nearly the truth if I said in a complete state of unpreparedness. The best prepared of the allied countries never dreamt of the terrific onslaught which was launched against liberty, humanity .and civilization in August, 1914. None realized at first the awful significance of that outbreak, least of all, perhaps, the people of the dominions beyond the seas. We were safely and snugly situated, many thousands of miles from the actual 6cene of conflict. Our first enrolment in Canada proceeded upon the principle of voluntary enlistment. In Great Britain, after the regular army had been utilized, volunteers were called for until that system had reached its limit, and I think the system we adopted in Canada was adopted also in every other of the selfgoverning British dominions. In Canada, the first call for volunteers met with what, in my opinion, was a magnificent response;
33,000	men responded within six weeks, an equal or larger number in the next'four or five weeks, and well do I remember, in the short session of August, 1914, standing on the corner of McLeod and Elgin streets, Ottawa, when we saw the Princess Patricias march proudly past. Well do I remember, on the 25th August, standing in front of the old Parliament Buildings, when we all cheered for the men from British Columbia, who were in service ready to go to the front just about twenty days after the call had gone forth for volunteers-and splendid fellows they were, many of whom have fought their last fight. They certainly answered the call in the most speedy and noblest fashion. I know that it is chafrged by many that our system of voluntary enlistment was a great blunder from the beginning, and that at the very outset we should have taken a course such as that recently adopted in the United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, we are all inclined to be very wise after the fact. It may be quite true that the United States has gone about the question of enrolment in a better manner than that adopted by us.
But the United States has had the opportunity of profiting by our experience and the experience of many other countries. In August, 1914, I think we were all in accord with the voluntary system being

the proper system of enlistment in Canada. So far as my recollection goes, no one suggested any other system. If in our decision we blundered, the blunder was confined not to Canada alone; it took place in every other British Dominion. But I do not agree with any critic who says that the voluntary system in Canada has been in any degree a failure; I rather think that from beginning to end it has been a magnificent success. But conditions have changed since August 1914. Perhaps I might illustrate that change by relating an incident that occurred during the short session of 1914. I well remember a remark made by one of the two Conservative friends with whom I walked one day down the broad way leading from the Parliament Buildings. He said: If I were Prime Minister, my policy would be, $100,000,000 and
100,000	men-and I would dissolve Parliament and go to the country on that policy. But the other man said: No; what is the use of promising something that you cannot perform? It looked like a monstrous promise at that time; we did not know what was before us. Let me give you another instance. We thought we were doing mighty well in August, 1914, when we made a contribution to the Mother Country of a million sacks of flour. We thought that that was wonderful-and under ordinary circumstances it would have been wonderful. Little did we dream then of the conflict that was to come; little did we anticipate then the millions of dollars that we should contribute and the hundreds of thousands of men who should leave Canada. I mention these matters merely to show that we thought somewhat lightly of the war or of the prospects of a lengthy conflict when we first started upon a volunteering system.
The charge so often made that our system of volunteering has fallen down is, in my judgment, absolutely unfounded. The voluntary system is a good system, but like all other human systems, it has its limitations. I am inclined to think that we have now come almost to the limit of that system in Canada. I have been pretty much of that opinion since last November or December, about the time of the campaign on behalf of national service. The figures in Tespect of volunteering were falling off very rapidly. I myself held meetings in the campaign for national service, and I heard many \ expressions of opinion in Tegard to what the 'Government should do in the way of securing more recruits. In fact, when I came to Ottawa at the opening of
