this session I had a motion prepared on the very question of conscription. When I came back after the adjournment I learned that my hon. friend (Sir Sam Hughes) had placed such a motion on the Order Paper. Knowing full well that the remarks of a man of his standing and knowledge on this subject would have far more force and effect than anything that I could say, I thought no more of the matter.
To my mind, this is not a new question. Last spring recruiting in Canada had fallen so low that we did not have sufficient recruits to make up the actual wastage in Canada. Any man who has the war at heart-and I believe we all have the war at heart-must acknowledge that Government or Parliament must take some definite step to get more men, and to get them as speedily as they can be procured.

What strike's me from these two statements ,is, that we have ample power in Canada if we can utilize it, and the purpose of this Bill, if I understand it aright, is to utilize that manpower, not only for military purposes, but for all the necessary purposes in connee-tion with the war.
I am gping for a moment or two to discuss one or two sections of the Militia Act which seem to have given rise to some controversy in this House. I was always under the impression that under the Militia Act the Government could, in the case of an emergency, call out and send abroad to any quarter of the world all the manhood of Canada from eighteen to sixty years of age, simply upon an Order in Council and upon another condition that, if Parliament was not then in session, Parliament should be convened within fifteen days thereafter. I believe I was correct in that impression and that I am correct now. At the time of Confederation, at least in 1868, the law was that all the male population from eighteen to sixty years of age could thus be called out. I remember when the amendment to that Act was before the House in 1904 and the discussion that took place on that occasion. If my memory serves me aright, because I have not looked up the debate, on that occasion we added a clause especially relating to service of Canadians abroad on the order of the Governor in Council, and we placed in the statute that condition that Parliament must be convened within fifteen days after any such order was issued. That section, which is section 71 of the Militia Act and which is still in force in Canada, reads:
Whenever the Governor in Council places the militia, or any part thereof, on active service, if Parliament is then separated by such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall he issued for the meeting of Parliament within fifteen days,, and Parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such pro-

clamation, and- shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
The reference in the section is to 4 Ed. VII, chapter 23, section 71. That section was placed in the Militia Act of Canada when my right hon. leader was the head of the 'Government and I, one of his humble supporters. That law has remained in force ever since, and if my memory serves me aright, when the Naval Service Bill was before the House in 1910, a special section was inserted in that Bill and the defence of the section by those who approved it, when it was attacked by those who objected to it, was that they had inserted the precise language of the Militia Act in the Nav-al Service Bill. I am prepared to stand by that section at the present itime. So far as the conscription of men is concerned, there is wider and more drastic power in the Militia Act of Canada passed in 1868 and amended in 1904 than there is in the Military Service Bill now before this House. The only objection I have to that power is that it is too drastic. The Governor General, on the advice of his Cabinet, could, under that Act, call out the whole male population of Canada between eighteen and sixty years of age and could send them overseas, but I doubt very much if he could call them out for any other purpose than military -service. It might be possible that, under the guise of the term " Military Service," -men might be employed in the mines, or railroads, or other industries of that description, but the meaning of the law is that those who are called out shall be utilized for military purposes. That power is on the statute book, and it is a power that the Government can utilize today. What is the objection to the old Militia Act? Simply that we want to avoid conscripting men for a single purpose. We want to provide that every purpose pertaining to the war shall be supplied, and, to my -mind, that is the chief feature in this Military Service Bill. We have been told by parliamentarians, by the press of the country, from the pulpit and at almost any meeting one can go to in any city, town, or village, that one of the first duties of this country is to produce foodstuffs. The farmers have been told, through their farm newspapers and through the general press; it has been dinned into everybody's ears, and everyone in this House knows that one of the great demands in this country, from the Atlantic to the,Pacific, to-day is -for agricultural labour. The men from the townships of Ontario have not volunteered in

the same proportion as men from the cities, but I can speak best of the county of South Wellington, whence I come, and I know that not only in South Wellington, but in North Wellington every. township is well represented in the infantry battalions and batteries at the front. They have contributed their full share, and what is the result? On every hand we hear the cry for hired help. Last week I returned home, and a man of thirty years of age, with 250 acres of land and 80 head of fine cattle, but with no hired help, said to me: " What has conscription to do for me? Is conscription going to take me?" I said: "No." He named in the county of Halton a farmer with two sons who owned 100 acres of land, and my suggestion would be: Might not conscription bring one of these sons from the small farm to the man who had 250 acres and no hired help?
Where does the Bill provide for that?

In the selective feature. At least I have so argued and so understood. If men who enroll for service under the Military Service law are better adapted for agricultural service than for military service, agricultural service is what they will be put to.
That is not provided for in the Bill.

Then that is a detail that should be remedied, but I understand that is the real purport of the Bill, and I have told some of my agricultural friends that in so>
many words. I do not believe you can get another man to-day from the farms of western Ontario without injuring the production which we say is only second in regard to our necessities for the war-men at the front coming first and production second. That is one reason why I prefer the Military Service Bill to the present Militia Act.
I believe there is a large number of men available in the cities and towns and villages of Canada who cannot be reached except by this Bill. I have probably addressed more recruiting and Patriotic Fund meetings in the province of Ontario than any other member of the House, except perhaps the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, and any one who has tried as hard as I have must have come to the conclusion that the men whom you want to reach are the very ones who do not attend recruiting meetings. At one town
in western Ontario somewhat of a joke was perpetrated not long ago. A recruiting meeting at the market house was to be addressed by a sergeant from the lower provinces. He was an excellent speaker, but as there were hardly any men present the meeting was adjourned, and the recruiting sergeant received permission from the manager of the picture show at the other end of the town to make his speech there. Many of the men at the theatre felt quite insulted and complained to the manager that if such a thing ever occurred again they would no longer patronize his show. The fact is, the men you want to enroll do not attend the recruiting meetings. I am speaking only of the places I know best, and am not referring to other parts of Canada at all. I am sure that if this Bill is passed a great many men now in Guelph will go to the front and probably volunteer before conscription comes in. I look in the banks and see able-bodied male clerks doing women's work. I see them also in the dry goods and retail stores, in the counting houses and a dozen other places where female labour could easily do the work. These men cannot be aroused to enlist either by personal interview or by speeches at meetings. I think there is no way of getting them unless by some measure of force. The city of Guelph with a population of 18,000, has given almost 10 per cent of her population, or about 1,700 men. That is a pretty good showing for a town of that size, but there are still 300 or 400 more men in that city who could be reached by a measure of this kind, and who will not come forward unless compulsion is used. I suppose conditions are much the same in other cities throughout Canada
I much prefer this Bill to the Militia Act. I am in favour of it because, for one reason, it will enable every necessary branch of labour to be supplied. In this connection I wish to refer to a circular which I think has been sent to every member of the 'House from the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, dated June 11, 1917. This circular comes from a body of men for whom I have the highest respect and regard. During the seventeen years I have sat in the House there have been very few occasions upon which I have not been able to see eye to eye with the'Trades and Labour Congress of Canada. I believe that union labour in Canada represents an exceedingly valuable body of our population. Not only are they good workers, but clear
/

and level-headed men of good judgment and common sense. Sometimes they make mistakes as other people do, and I believe that in this circular they are labouring under some misapprehension. There is not a great deal of difference between the Trades and Labour Congress and myself in regard to this circular; in fact, we are very close together except on one point. One paragraph of the circular says, under the heading of Conscription:
On December 27th, 1916, Premier Borden informed the executive of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, that if conscription should prove the only effective method to preserve the existence of the State and of the institutions and liberties which we enjoy, I should not hesitate to act accordingly.
The Trades and Labour Congress followed that up with this clause of their own:
We are positively of the opinion that this situation has not arrived.
With that statement I certainly take issue. The next paragraph says:
The necessities for the effective conduct of the war are food, munitions, shipping, and military man power, and Canada is geographically well situated to supply the first named three essentials, and can do much to assist in winning the war by developing her production in these essentials to her fullest extent.
The only exception I take to that is the order in which the necessities are put. They have put last what I would put first, namely, military man power. I would entirely agree with them if the order were reversed thus:	military man power, food,
munitions and shipping. I entirely disagree with them when they say that the time has not arrived, and I believe that when the Trades and Labour Congress thoroughly understand the situation they will see that I am right and they are wrong. If I were simply to endorse their statement- and that is their statement-they would have mighty little respect for me and I would have mighty little Tespect for myself. Union labour in this country has furnished our forces with a tremendous number of men. It is entitled to very great credit for what it has done to back up our men at the front and' our war operations generally. But we have now evidently reached a line of cleavage, and upon this question I and my friends of the Trades and Labour Congress do not -agree. I believe that the time has come for putting a Military Service Bill into force; the Trades and Labour Congress take the opposite view, that the time has not yet arrived.
[Mr. Guthrie.!
There is another organization with which I have not so much sympathy, known as the British Columbia Federation of Labour, and -another organization known as the Social-Democratic Party of Canada. The British Columbia Federation of Labour went on record as being opposed- to conscription on the general proposition that:
Military or industrial conscription is the imposition of a form of servitude which is obnoxious to a so called free people.
I do not think it is worth while taking up the time of the House discussing propositions of that kind. So far as the Social-Democratic party in this country is concerned I take no interest in it. I do not think it is helpful in any way. Mr. Speaker, just before six o'clock, I was endeavouring to discuss some of the selective features of the Militia Bill which is now before the House. My attention was called during the adjournment to some of the language which I used, and on further examination of the Bill, I concluded that perhaps my language in regard to agricultural labour was broader than the terms of the Bill would warrant. I notice that the Bill in its preamble mentiohs the question of agricultural labour and says:
.TUNE 19, 1917
And whereas, by reason of the large number of men who have already left agricultural and industrial pursuits in Canada to join such Expeditionary Force as volunteers, and of the necessity of sustaining under such conditions the productivity of the Dominion, it is expedient to secure the men still required, not by ballot as provided in the Militia Act, but by selective draft.
Then on referring to section 11 of the Bill I find it provides that:
An application may be made, by or in respect of any man in the class or subclass called out by such proclamation to a local tribunal established in the province in which such man ordinarily resides, for a certificate of exemption on any of the following grounds:-
(a) That it is expedient in the national interest that the man should, instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he is habitually engaged;
(b) That it is expedient in the national interest that the man should, instead of being employed in military service, be engaged in other work in which he wishes to be engaged and for which he has special qualifications.
I must say that on reading this section again, the language I used before adjournment at six o'clock seems to he rather too broad. My understanding. of the Bill at that time was that, under the selective system, a board would have (power to supply agricultural labour just to the same extent as it would have power to tell a man to serve in the military forces. On reading the Act more carefully, I find that this exemption is to be granted only at the request of the man himself. I think that is a detail of the Bill which may well be looked into, and amended, if necessary, when we come to the' committee stage. In every city, town , and village in Ontario, farm labour has become scarce for two reasons: First, by reason of enlistment; and, secondly, by reason of the attractive wages paid by manufacturing companies during the present war, and particularly by munition factories. If a man, by making an application, can continue earning $4, $5 or $6 a day in a munition factory, he will not, as a matter of choice, return to the farm, although he is especially qualified to do farm work. I think the board having control of these matters should certainly be entitled to conscript that man's work, and have him engage in agricultural labour if he is not going forward for military purposes. That was my understanding of the Bill when I spoke, and if it is not the letter of the Bill, I think it should be made plain, because the farmers are suffering very gravely from the want of help from the two causes I have mentioned. I maintain that the farmer in the back concession of a back township who makes two blades of grass
grow this year where but one grew last year, is doing a patriotic duty, and is serving his country to the utmost of his capacity. That man needs help and should be helped, and there should be something in this Bill to supply him with labour ordinarily called agricultural labour, which has flocked to the cities, towns and villages, where manufacturing industries pay much higher wages than are paid in the country. This is the sacrifice the individual will have to make.
There are other great lines of industry that may have to be helped also. I doubt very much if you will get very many men from the transportation companies or from shipping companies. I hear on every hand that men are becoming scarcer and scarcer upon the railways, and that great difficulty will be experienced this year in securing crews for both lake and ocean shipping. It may be that, for transportation purposes, men may have to be taken from [DOT] other callings, and I think that the board dealing with these matters should be given power under this Act to arrange to furnish a supply of labour for transportation and shipping companies. There is, of course, a great deal of necessary and essential labour that must be performed in Canada. We are dependent for our food, our raiment, and our shelter, and need a tremendous number of men, whose services will be required for 'the production of articles required for consumption in Canada alone. Notwithstanding that, there are so many industries in Canada to-day that are producing what at any time we would call luxuries, in addition to the men whom I mentioned earlier in my address, that I have no doubt the classes enumerated 'in the first four section of this Bill will readily yield all the men that are necessary, and more, within the present year at all events, for military purposes, and that the different industries which are essential to the proper carrying on of the war may all likewise be supplied.
Now a word in regard to the amendment moved by my right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) upon the question of a referendum. Upon this point I cannot agree with the view taken by my leader. I have never been favourable to the principle of referendum. I think it is antagonistic to our ideas of responsible Government. We are elected to this House by our electors to pass necessary legislation, to adopt necessary measures, according to the judgment and ability which we have, and if we make mistakes, if we blunder, if we do wrong, our responsibility is directly to our electors, who can



turn us out at the first ensuing general election.
If you adopt the principle of a referendum, you are going to find the Government of Canada in this position: that upon every difficult question the Government will adopt the referendum if, for no other purpose than to avoid any conflict of opinion in regard to itself. Our system is, and has always been, founded upon the doctrine of responsibility. The Government is responsible to Parliament and the people; and members of Parliament are responsible to the people, and if the people desire a change they have a right to make it. While it is said the system of referendum and of initiative and recall are more or less favoured, particularly in the Western States, and to 6ome extent in the western provinces of Canada, I believe the constitutional method of dealing with the question is for Parliament to decide it, and the people then have the right to review our work at each general election. My right hon. leader took that course on more than one occasion, notably in 1911, on the reciprocity issue. He might have had a referendum on that r question and continued to hold power, but I submit that would not have been'constitutional and not good British parliamentary practice in that case, nor would it be good practice at the present time. I remember also', when the Navy debate took place in the House, in 1910, the question of referendum was brought up once more. My right hon. leader might have sheltered himself under the referendum, instead of allowing himself to be involved upon this question in the election of 1911. But he took the course a statesman would take, and said, "No, when the time comes we will appeal to the people," and he did appeal to the people, and on that and other issues, was defeated. The Government takes its own course in these matters, and if blunders or mistakes are made, the Government is responsible to the people. For that broad reason, I do not favour a referendum.
Then, again, I think, upon this question a referendum is entirely unnecessary. In my view of the matter, the first duty of the people, and the first duty of Parliament, is to defend their country. That is a natural duty, a natural right, one that we are bound to assume and perform. If we take our oath of loyalty, we assume that obligation. We require no mandate for the performance of a paramount duty.
Another objection is that, instead of threshing the question out in this House-

and it is a difficult question-we would transfer the contest to the platforms of this country, where it would be a more difficult question and might cause very serious disturbance. There is no reason for referring it for decision to the electors. Why not, in a manly way, settle it ourselves? I believe also that it is not possible at the present time to have a fair referendum. I would never consent under any conditions to have a referendum which did not include the men who have volunteered and gone abroad in the 'Service of the country. If my memory serves me, the total vote in the election of 1911 was about 1,200,000. When you consider that something over 400,000 have enlisted, that means that 33 per cent of your electorate is out of Canada. How are you going to take the vote of these men r It cannot be taken. When the Soldiers* Bill was introduced by the present Government I was suffering from illness and was not in the House, but I thought if ever a Government went the extreme length in trying to poll the soldier vote, it was the present Government. I did not believe at the time that the Government was serious, nor that they would poll that vote if they could. But apart from that, is it possible to take the soldiers vote, are-you going to poll the vote of the men in France? Are you going to cease firing and pass the ballot boxes around? You must remember there are 136,000 loyal Canadians at the firing line. How are you going to take the soldiers' vote in England, where we -have 28,000 troops at present, probably-on their way to the front, and 80,000 intraining, the balance being in hospitals and convalescent homes. Do you think that vote could be polled? What have you on this side of the water? You have a population which says, "We will not enlist." Do hon. gentlemen think that men who will not enlist will support a compulsion on referendum? The proposition would be defeated. The -men who did not want to go to defend their country would vote -against it. I do not think that would be a fair vote. I believe, if any one is entitled- to vote on this question, it is the men who are overseas, and I see no way of fairly taking their votes without a tremendous expenditure of time, if it be possible to take it at -all, I believe that is one-fundamental reason for opposing a referendum upon this question. Never would I consent to have a -slacker at home vote,, and a man at the front be deprived of his, vote.
Hear, hear.

However, the difficulty can be overcome in another way. If you allow this Bill to pass without a referendum, you may consult the people afterwards, when the boys come home. You may then get some fair expression of opinion on the question, which I do not believe you can ever obtain until the war is over, and the boys return. A referendum to my mind would leave the decision of one of the most vital questions which has arisen in Canada to the very people who have neglected to volunteer, and to the parents of those who are so timid as not to permit their sons, who would otherwise volunteer, to enlist for service. I will never consent to have the question submitted to such an electorate.
These are, substantially, my reasons for opposing the amendment moved by my right hon. friend, and leader. He has referred to another question, which I will discuss very, very briefly; that is that this Parliament is in the nature of a moribund Parliament, or, as he described it,, a rump Parliament, his contention being that, on that ground, this House should not deal with it.
I do not take that view of the matter. My view is that this Parliament is in every respect legally constituted. I do not think that I am telling any secrets or betraying any confidences when I say that in February, 1916, I was about the only man on this side of the House, except some members from the province of Quebec, who were opposed to the first extension of the term of Parliament. I thought that there should be no extension. I pointed out then to my friends: if you grant extension this year, what are you going to do next year, when the war may be more serious than ever? Last year we on this side of the House committed ourselves unanimously to the granting of an extension. Both Houses of Parliament agreed to the extension and the British Government, as our supreme authority, amended the British North America Act so as to extend the life of Parliament for one year. That extension was strictly constitutional; it did not limit our authority in any way. If anything, it was an enabling Act, to enable us to carry on our national affairs. It could not and did not restrict our rights; every Act that we could legally pass a year ago we can just as legally pass to-day. The Parliament of Canada sitting here to-day is legally constituted for all purposes and

can deal with full power and authority with the Military Service Bill or with any other Bill which may be brought before it. The question is as to the wisdom or the propriety of any course that is proposed and not as to our constitutional right to pass this, that, or 'the other Bill.
. I have noticed in the newspapers during this month the reports of many of the church congresses of Canada which usually meet in the month of June. I have read the report of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian church in Canada, representative of that church from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I have read the reports of the Methodist Conferences held in various parts of the Dominion; of the annual meetings of the Baptist church, and of various meetings of the Anglican Synods. - Speaking generally, each of those church courts has passed almost unanimously motions in support of the present Military Service Bill. In some cases they have added that which I believe to be exceedingly important, namely, that wealth and other resources should likewise be conscripted; but in no>
case have I seen anything like a proposal for a referendum or a general election. The Minister of Public Works (Hon. Robert Rogers) in the month of June, 1915, put his ear to the ground and heard murrnur-ings and rumblings, which gradually increased to tones of thunder, and he told us that the people demanded an immediate election. I may tell the hon. gentleman that if he puts his ear to the ground now he will still hear murmurings and rumblings, growing louder and louder until they become like tones of thunder. They ask, however, not for a general election, Ibut that we have no general election at the present time. A referendum on this question would' be the equivalent to a general election, and to that I am opposed.
It is asked, is there any demand for a Conscription Bill of this kind? Apart from the church courts, the municipal bodies, and the boards of trade that have passed on the question, I do not know that there is any general demand among the people on the subject. We have read reports of meetings at Toronto and elsewhere, at which resolutions endorsing the principle of this Bill have 'been adopted, but I do not know that among the people themselves there has been any general demand for such legislation; in fact, I am inclined to believe that the demand has been the other way. I havq received only a few letters on the subject, and none of them have been decided in

their expressions of opinion, and none of them have been signed. I think that there are a good many people who do not want to show their hands in regard to conscription. My suggestion would be that if we are to have a referendum on it,.the people should vote as we vote in this Parliament, by standing up, or showing their hands. I would favour the old open vote, in order that we may know just where the people stand with regard to the referendum. I have not received any petitions against the proposal except the one directed to me by the Trades and Labour Council. But there certainly is an urgent call for men. Every man on this side of the House knows it; every man on the other side knows it. The question is, how are we 'going, to get them? So far, nobody has told us; nobody has suggested how we shall get the necessary men-that is, aside from the adoption of this Bill or the enforcement of the Militia Act. I thought, perhaps, my right hon. friend and leader might make some suggestion, but he did not. Perhaps as the debate goes on some suggestion may come from somebody, but personally I see no way of getting more men unless we adopt some compulsory system.
There is a clause in the proposed measure which .provides that the legislation shall come into force upon the proclamation of the Governor General in Council. Whether that is a wise proposal I do not know. I would prefer that .a definite date be fixed, *say two or three months hence, rather than that the coming into force of the Act should be left altogether to the whim of the Government. If a date two or three months hence were fixed and the Bill were passed the result might have a good effect upon recruiting. There is no doubt that after the Prime Minister made his first statement in the House with regard to conscription, a larger number of recruits presented themselves at the various recruiting offices than had been the case for some time previously. I am sorry to say that the results of the presentation of recruits was not in all cases very satisfactory. In one case where 29 men presented themselves .two days after the speech delivered by the Prime Minister the local board who examined them rejected 23 as medically unfit and accepted 6. Another board in another city passed upon the same 29 men on the following day and reversed the figures, accepting 23 and rejecting 6. The Prime Minister must safeguard this Bill in that respect. Local influences may and will be used; I am strongly opposed to the appointment of anything like local

boards. It will not cost much to establish boards here and there in different places throughout the Dominion and move them from time to time so there may be no chance of partiality in their decisions. That is my only reason for mentioning this matter.
But, as I have said, the call throughout Canada and the world is for men. The call comes from every quarter; it comes from the men in the trenches and in the hospitals, from the returned soldiers and perhaps also from the dead. There is no doubt that the people of Canada are under the most solemn pledge that men or women could give to support the men who have gone into the trenches; we cannot avoid that responsibility whatever else we may avoid. I shall place on the records of this House a poem of noble thought and sublime inspiration which tells of that call from the dead. A young man, a school friend of mine, Jack McCrea, of Guelph, now as Captain John McCrea, serving at the front with a detachment from McGill University, is the author of this now celebrated poem. It was first published in Punch in London and was afterwards copied in many British, American and Canadian newspapers. One paper said it was perhaps as pure a bit of poetry as had ever been written in the English language. Another paper said that there was more direct appeal in the few lines than there would be in a volume of large dimensions. These lines, I believe, should be in every school-book in. this country, and I read them that they may be printed in Hansard:
In Flanders' Fields.
In Flanders fields the poppies blow Between the crosses, row on row,
That mark our place, and in the sky The larks still bravely singing-, fly, Scarce heard amidst the guns below.
We are the Dead. Short days ago We lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow, Loved and were loved, and now we lie In Flanders' fields.
Take up our quarrel with the foe,
To you from falling hands we throw The torch,-be yours to hold it high ;
If ye break faith with us who die,
We shall not sleep though poppies grow In Flanders' fields.
Surely, in those beautiful words, there is an appeal from the dead. There is a condition which we must meet soon, or it will not be very long before Canada is unrepresented at the front. I have my own ideas on this matter, and I am going to conclude by stating them.
Perhaps I stand by myself on this question, but for a long time I have been and

still am in favour of co-operation between the parties in this House, not only at the present moment, but as long as the war lasts. I favour coalition; I favour an extension of the term of Parliament, and I favour this Bill. I do not believe this Bill will be successfully put in force by a single political party; I fear it will not. We are all agreed that we must have men. I have read very carefully the correspondence which has passed between the Prime Minister and my right hon. friend and leader on the question of a coalition Government. To the ordinary mind, no insurmountable objection was presented in the correspondence, nothing that a little compromise could not overcome. We have certain facts before us, and we are all agreed on them. On the one hand we have on the statute book now a Militia Act which can be enforced at any time and which is more stringent in its terms than the present Military Service Bill. On the other hand, we have the Military Service Bill providing for conscription on the principle of selection. If I read the correspondence aright, the leaders of the parties in this House could not come together on the single question of conscription. As I have said, I do not consider that an insurmountable objection; I believe if the two leaders really intended to agree, they could agree upon this question. There must be some give and take, some compromise in such a matter. Why not have a consolidation of the two Bills, leaving the Canada Militia Act practically as it stands, but adding to it the selective clauses of the present measure? Conscrip-tive legislation is on the statute book now; we are neither introducing nor passing it. It is there and has been since 1868. The selective clauses are new. I am quite satisfied that the Prime Minister has no thirst to hold on to power, and I am just as confident that on the part of my right hon. friend and leader that he has no keen desire to attain power. I believe both leaders are both absolutely sincere, but something which I think could be and should be overcome, stands between them. What an example it would be to the whole of this country if the two great political parties came together and settled their differences. I do not mean past disputes; I do not mean questions of the management or mismanagement of the war in the past three years; I mean that only from this time forward. If an agreement could be reached on the main question and nothing taken up save
measures which pertain to the war, it would be a happy day for Canada. Then after the war, we can fight out our differences.
I cannot approve the suggestion of the Prime Minister, as set out in the correspondence, that a coalition should be formed; that this Bill should be passed, and then that an appeal be made to the people for a mandate. What we want to avoid is a general election, not to bring one on, what we should do is to come together and have the term of Parliament extended and carry this war to a successful conclusion, and then if the people condemn us, let them condemn us and turn us out. So long as we have done our duty, we need not fear. The time is not too late for the leaders to come together. This matter is so serious that I can scarcely put my thoughts into language. I know that in every corner of Canada the people would approve it if our leaders came together. This Bill, if it is passed, is going to get us nowhere; no one party will be able to enforce it successfully; it will cause strife and discord in many parts of Canada. Perhaps if some of those less prominent members on either side of the House were to take up the matter of coalition it might not be a bad thing. I believe that all the brains of this House of Commons are not to be found on the front benches of either party. Perhaps if a few of us back-benchers could sit down for half an hour or an hour, we might work out something feasible which our leaders might accept, but I most sincerely ask that negotiations be not concluded at the present time and that another effort may be made to secure coalition. I know there has in the past been a great deal said, particularly in the newspapers, which is hard to overlook; that insult has been heaped upon insult by the press of both parties. These things sting and smart; but when we are face to face with a fight to a finish, with a world conflict, when my leader's sentiments are that Canada is in this war "to the last ditch" and, some years ago "to the last man and the last dollar," and when these are also the sentiments of the Prime Minister, surely these worthy gentlemen can come together on this question, upon some ground acceptable to all Canadians.
If not, could not a committee be got together which might perform some useful services? There need be no quarrel over names In any coalition government; put it on the basis of the members of His Majesty's Privy Council in Canada. There are plenty

o;f able men of the Privy Council in this House well qualified for .office. Let them get together and set about to win the war. When the war is won let us have a general election, and if the people do not approve the arrangement they can turn it out of power. That is my suggestion, and I make it as seripusly as ever I spoke in my life.

If I am asked what we are fighting for I can reply in two sentences. In the first place to fulfill a solemn international obligation,- an obligation which if it had been entered into between private persons in the ordinary concerns of life would have been regarded as an obligation not only of law but of honour which no self-respecting man could possibly have repudiated. The reasons Mr. Asquith gave at the beginning of the war why Great Britain came into this stupendous struggle hold good to-day, and the Canadian people, whether they belong to the French-speaking or English-speaking nationalities, stand and abide by those lofty principles. Let me read the section, because I believe	my	hon.	friend	from	South
Wellington was in error when he argued that the principal change at the time of the revision of the Militia Act in 1904 was made in section 71. There were three chief modifications of the Militia Act as brought down by the late Sir Frederick Borden in 1904. The first was one concerning the commanding officer of the Canadian militia. Until the year 1904 the command of the militia had to be given to a British officer, whilst since 1904 the command can be given to a Canadian military officer. The other change has regard to the raising of the militia of Canada in times of emergency to be sent without the country. The change made in that clause consists in the addition of the words "for the defence thereof." Let me read that section-

The Governor in Council may place the militia, or any part thereof, on active service anywhere in Canada, and also beyond Canada, for the defence thereof-
These words were added. They were not in the old statute. They were added for a reason which I shall explain in a moment.
-for the defence thereof, at any time when it appears advisable so to do by reason of emergency.
The third modification was made 'by section 71, and it has reference to the calling of Parliament. It reads as followsi;
Whenever the Governor in Council places the militia, or any part (hereof, on active service, if Parliament is then separated hy such adjournment or prorogation as will not expire within ten days, a proclamation shall he issued for the meeting of Parliament within fifteen days, and Parliament shall accordingly meet and sit upon the day appointed by such proclamation, and shall continue to sit and act in like manner as if it had stood adjourned or prorogued to the same day.
Nobody takes exception to that very wise clause having been inserted in the Militia Act. It is not in question, at all events. I have not his words here, but Sir Charles Fitzpatrick would not have said otherwise than did the statute, which is very clear. Besides, Sir Frederick Borden was very emphatic. The hon. gentleman has asked with an affectation ot much anxiety, what the world will think, and what the rest of the British Empire will think of Canada-though I have told him over and over again that upon the Statute-book of every colony of the British Empire is to be found precisely the same provision as he is now criticising. And. Sir, upon the Statute-book of the Mother -Country herself, the hon. gentleman will find this section 12, part 3 (presumably of the Army Act) "any part of the militia shall be liable to serve in any part of the United Kingdom; but no part of the militia shall be carried or ordered to go out of the United Kingdom."
So that in every British colony, in every province before Confederation, even in the Mother Cbumtry, militia troops could not be dispatched outside of the territory except for the defence of the territory itself. That case is made abundantly clear. And, Mr. Speaker, why should we be discussing this point? Has not the Prime Minister himself, as was made so evident yesterday by the dispatch Tead by the right hon. leader of the Opposition, admitted the force of the view taken by Sir Frederick Borden as he introduced that legislation in 1904? He said through the Governor General to the home Government that Canada contemplated aiding the Mother Country in that great struggle, but that, unfortunately, they were handicapped as to their right to dispatch troops outside of our own territory. As a result, Sir, an Order in Council was passed at the request of this Government by the Imperial authorities incorporating our troops into the Imperial army. This fact is unchallenged, and I do not see the object of discussing whether or not constitutionally we have a right to send our men outside of Canada except for the defence of our own country. I do not say that Canada will not, I do not say that Canada may not, but that Canada must, makes in my opinion, all the difference in the world.
Sir, on this grave issue I stand upon the bedrock of our constitution, and I claim that England has accepted the Canadian contention that there is no constitutional obligation upon us to take part in wars outside of Canada, except for the defence of our territory. I am proud to say that we
have taken part in this stupendous struggle for liberty, but it is on the principle of the voluntary system, and it is on that principle that I, as a Canadian, desire that Canada shall continue to the end to be with the Allies. I may say at once to the father confessor of the Tory party, my good friend, the Solicitor General, that I am opposed to compulsory service, and I do not understand his anxiety in asking every member on this side of the House to state whether he will support conscription or be against it, if a referendum be submitted. I say to him that conscription for Canada is the Milner system-the autocratic system.
Hear, hear.

Every man in this free British country has a right to his own opinions, and has as much right to be against the compulsory system as has the Quaker, the Mennonite, aye, as much right to his opinion as Sir John Simon, Mr. John Mor-ley. No one either will question my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) the right to his opinion in favour of the compulsory system.
Hear, hear.

I am opposed to compulsory service, and why? We have entered this war on the principle of voluntary service, and the pledge of the Government to that effect is positive, direct and binding. The honour of Canada, the honour of the Government are at stake. The Prime Minister and his colleagues, from the highest to the humblest, have repeated, from one end of the country to the other, the statement that there would be no conscription in Canada.
Hear, hear.

They have repeated it
in public meetings, on every platform; they have repeated it here time and again before the assembled Parliament. I need not quote the pledges of the Prime Minister, as he will not deny them. Shall I say, Sir, that when the National Service cards were issued, the Prime Minister authorized some of his colleagues to declare that the people might sign those cards as they did not mean compulsory service. I say to him that he has authorized some of his colleagues to make that declaration to the Archbishop of Montreal, who issued a letter, inviting the faithful of Montreal to sign the National Service cards, because, he had the assurance .that they did not mean compulsory service. He distinctly accepted

the pledge and the word of honour of the Government that there would be no compulsory service. In what position to-day is that dignitary of the Church?
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend, the
Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Sevigny) stated in the county of Dorchester, to his electors a few weeks ago, that there would be no conscription. Mr. Speaker, you have in these well poised sentences the explanation of a peculiar psychology. There it is pointed out how it happens that, instinctively, the British-born were first to respond to the call; then the English Canadians and then the French Canadians.
I have said on many other occasions, and I repeat this evening, that recruiting is largely, if not wholly,' carried on successfully in urban centres. The province of Ontario is dotted with industrial bentres. In the province of Quebec, outside of Sherbrooke, Three Rivers. Sorel, Montreal and Quebec, we have few or little industrial centres. Quebec is a mostly rural province, and bear in mind that she gets no influx of immigration from the old country.
Mr. Speaker, I will with your leave complete the statement I have made to the House this evening in all frankness and sincerity. Sir, no effort worthy of the name has been made to intelligently recruit in the province of Quebec since the beginning of the war.
Some hon.. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen know
that from the session of Parliament in 1914
I urged the Government to appoint General Lessard as recruiting agent. He is the best and most qualified officer, and a man in whose judgment and ability our people have all confidence. Yet, General Lessard was only appointed on the 29th March, 1917, and my hon. friends will be honest enough to grant that all that delay was due to some bickerings and quarrels which happened at the time of the Boer war between General Lessard and the Minister of Militia and Defence. Is that a motive which should have deferred the early appointment of General Lessard to promote recruiting in Quebec? Sir, we had another excellent officer, a veteran from South Africa, Colonel Pelletier, of Quebec, son of the late Lieutenant Governor, Sir Alphonse Pelletier. At the beginning of the war he was ignored and finally he was given his pension. There was in Montreal Colonel Roy, who was the district commanding officer. He knew our people, was trusted, and spoke the language of the majority. He was sent to British Columbia, and later on was pensioned and replaced by General Wilson of Montreal, who is a personal friend of mine, a gentleman, but who hardly speaks a word of French. I was chairman of the civilian committee of the Asselin regiment, and I must say, in all justice to my friend the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence, that he gave us, the French Canadians of Montreal, a most loyal support in the recruiting of that regiment. I thank him publicly to-day, as I thanked him publicly on many, many occasions previously. With the help received from his department, in less than two months, Major Asselin, who was very popular, who was exceedingly brilliant, succeeded in raising a regiment, but what hap-* pened? We founded great hopes, on that regiment. We expected that it would be the nucleus of many similar regiments in the province of Quebec. It was even hinted that my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Sevigny) would take a course at Kingston, in order to do as Major Asselin had dpne. What happened? Major Asselin's regiment was sent to Bermuda for several months. I do not blame the Government for that. There were military reasons, I suppose, for that action. Several other regiments have gone there. But what I and the people of Quebec resent is this: the regiment was transferred to a camp in Great Britain, I forget which camp, and, as soon as it reached Great Britain, the first order received by Major Asselin was that of the dislocation of his unit. It was divided



into several drafts and distributed amongst many regiments. The same fate happened to Colonel Piuze who raised a regiment in the district represented by my hon. friend the member fpr Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe). I know there are reasons for that and I do not blame the Government. But there is some pride in our people; they would have been glad' to read of the Asselin regiment at the front as the Asselin regiment, just as they were proud to hear of the 22nd battalion iat the front as the 22ncL battalion. True it is that there may have been military reasons for disbanding the battalion, but it is to say the least most unfortunate that the Government did not see its way clear to do for the Asselin battalion what was done for the Irish Brigade that was raised in Montreal. Although that brigade had not the required numbers, its identity was maintained and it was* given a tour in Ireland to arouse the people in that country as well as the Irish people in Canada to the necessities of the hour. That was wise policy on the part of the Government.

What has been done
since with that brigade?
I do not know.

Neither do I.
Mr. H. B. (MORPHY:	Does the hon.
member not know that the matter of which he complains was one of serious complaint also throughout western Ontario, because of units from the various counties there being broken up toy reason of militia regulations and orders of tlhe British War Office? .
I quite understand that; I know it is a fact. But there is a distinction.
* None whatever.

Yes, there is, and my
hon, friend is too fair not to admit it. The battalions from Ontario which were scattered amongst other units in Great Britain were composed of men speaking the English language. They could be understood by the Welsh and Irish Fusiliers, the Durhams and the Yorks, that' were so jauntily mentioned this afternoon by the ex-Minister of Militia. But the men recruited by Major Asselin were young Freneh-Canadians, mostly speaking only the French language. The battalion was sent to England, and there dislocated, the men being spread amongst various

units where they did not understand the language; where they did not speak the language of their commanding officers. I will give my hon. friend another instance -and I hope that the member for Kingston will listen to me for a moment. This will give the House an idea of how something unfair may sometimes be done unwittingly. Last winter I was travelling from Quebec to Montreal. It was a bitterly cold evening. I was in a pullman car-although I am not a minister of the Crown, I sometimes travel in a pullman car. I noticed a young man, rather short and stocky, dressed in kilties. As I looked at him I said to myself: surely this is not a Highlander-yet he ha3 the kilties, and a Scotch cap. As I looked at him he also looked at me, and then addressing (him in French. I said: "Are you not a Scotchman?" He said: "No, I am Albert Martel, from Quebec." I said:	"Under
what guise are you travelling?" "Oh, well," he said, "I was in Ottawa; our regiment, which was being recruited by Colonel de Salaberry, was disbanded for certain reasons, and I offered my services to the Kingston Queen's Highlanders, which left a few weeks ago." What was the strength oi that unit?
About 700.

As Martel was passing from the pullman to the first class coaches, I said: "Where are you going?" He answered :	" To see my men." " Your men? "
" Yes," he said, " I am recruiting in Quebec for the Queen's Highlanders; I will introduce you to 17 Highlanders from Sir Wilfrid Laurier's constituency. I am going to Ottawa-it is not the shortest way to Kingston -but I am going there with my men because Ottawa is dry and I want to spend a Sunday in that place." They came to Ottawa, and I saw alighting from the train the 18 kilties, fine, bright fellows, not one of them speaking a word of English. That is the first chapter of my little story.
A few days ago the bell was rung at my residence. A gentleman in kilts was ushered in. " Bonjour, monsieur; I am Lieutenant Martel." " Oh," I said, " the gentleman I met this winter. Are you still recruiting for the Queen's Highlanders?" " I have recruited," he answered, " 101 men; they left a few weeks ago with a battalion made up of about 700 Scotchmen." " Did you not follow your men? " I asked. He answered: " No." Now there comes a blank in my story, tout if the member for Kingston will come to me after the sitting I will tell him why Lieutenant Mar-

tel di'd not follow his men, though he promised the fathers and mothers of those French-Canadian Highlanders that he would follow them to England. Bear in mind that they were confided to his care, because he spoke their language, because he understood them, because they and their families had confidence in him. At the last moment, for reasons which I will give my hon. friend-and which I gave to the Minister of Justice the other day, who told me since that I had a very good case indeed- Martel did not go. The men who left with the Highlanders will never be accounted as French-Oanadians from Quebec. Lieutenant Martel, who is in Ottawa, can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that 35 of his recruits do not speak a word of English; yet they are distributed among an English-speaking unit. I have faith in the Scotch. I love the Irish and I love the English, but I confess that I have a failing for the Scotch. These French-Canadians are in good company; I do not fear for them. But, Sir, do you not think that, in all fairness and in all justice, Lieutenant Albert Martel, who promised the fathers and mothers and relatives of these men that he would follow them to the last ditch, should have accompanied them when they marched off? I will not say why he did not accompany them.
Why do you not?
I will not; I will tell the member for Kingston. The reason is stated in the letters that I sent the other day to the Minister of Justice.
Does the hon. gentleman agree with the reasons given?
No.
You dissent from the reasons?
Certainly, and I will appeal to the fairness of my hon. friend when I tell him the facts.

Unless my hon. friend
thinks that on grounds of public policy those reasons should be kept secret, it might be just as well to remove this air of mystery. Perhaps I may be able to give him some information and enlightenment.

I will tell my hon. friend. I will now unbosom myself to the House in all sincerity and in all honesty of purpose. I do not see in the Chamber any hon. gentleman representing a Toronto constituency.
If one of them were here, I would say this: What would he think if I, being Minister of Militia, or better still, if the Minister of Inland Revenue being promoted to be Minister of Militia, were to appoint as chief recruiting agent for the city of Toronto the Superior of the Jesuit Order? With all due respect for the Jesuits and for my hon. friends from Toronto, would the Superior of the Jesuit Order have any success in the cause of recruiting in Toronto or say in Guelph, Kingston or St. Thomas? The answer is only too obvious. What has happened in Montreal? As I stated the other day to Marechal Joffre, the district and suburbs of Montreal are, outside of Paris and possibly Lyons in France, the-largest French district in the world. The' chief recruiting agent in Montreal, appointed by my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia, and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes), is. -a personal friend, of mine, but he is the *pastor of St. James Methodist chueh. He is a Liberal in principle; he is a home-ruler also. I have spoken with him in his own church, and I was taunted by some of my Catholic friends that I had turned Methodist, but as I was preaching for recruiting purposes, I was easily absolved. But, in all fairness and common sense, is it reasonable to expect that a Superior of .the Jesuits would meet with any success in recruiting in the city of Toronto, and is it to be expected that one of the ministers of the Methodist church would have any success in recruiting in a French and Catholic district like the district of Montreal? To put the question is to suggest the answer at once. That appointment was made, not for the purpose, I grant, of putting obstacles in the way of recruiting, but it was made all the same and there it is. I do not wish to impute motives to the ex-Minister of Militia.
Does he not get any English recruits in Montreal?

Yes, he has some English recruits, but does my hon. friend think it was conducive to bringing in French recruits which he and his friends say they expected from the province of Quebec, to so appoint a Methodist minister in that large French and Catholic district? It is useless to play upon words. My hon. friend must be credited with common sense. He might have appointed a Jesuit as recruiting officer in St. Boniface, but he would not have appointed a Jesuit in the city of Winnipeg. The matter is too self evident; it ' seems, Sir, as if every obstacle were put in
the way of recruiting in the province of Quebec.

Does my hon. friend not know of the opposite case where, for instance, Ontario regiments have had their officers taken away from them and have been put under French-Canadian officers? If he does not, I can give him some instances.

That is not the point at. all. I am speaking of the recruiting work, of the appeals made to the laymen to join the ranks. Those appeals were made in the English language; the recruits were merged into English-speaking units. The moment a French-Canadian officer speaks the English language, if he retains his rank and receives no favour, I see no objection to him taking command of an Englishspeaking regiment. In Quebec and Montreal, there have been and there are cases where the chief officers are English-speaking, and no objection is taken, far from it.

French-speaking officers
have been appointed in preference to English-speaking officers, and that has been done without objection in instances which I can quote to my hon. friend.

Certainly. There is no objection when there is no preferment, when it is only a matter of course. I do not object to an English officer having precedence over a French-Canadian officer if his rank will command that precedence. What I am pointing out is this: In the district of Montreal, the chief recruiting officer, a personal friend of mine, a charming, enlightened and great speaker for those who understand him, was a pastor of the Methodist church. The Minister of Militia and Defence might have done better if he had appointed a gentleman whose language and whose ambient air would have been more congenial to the men to whom he was appealing.
I have only a few words to add and it is on this question of a referendum. I will then conclude. This is of all measures the most vital that has ever been introduced into this Parliament; it is a departure from all our traditions; it means the alienation of human liberty; Parliament, functus officio, unrepresentative, moribund, with more than 20 seats vacant, with a West under-represented, cannot and dare not attempt to legislate for the people of Canada under such circumstances. There is only one solution and that is a referendum. The referendum, it is true, is more familiar

to Latin than to British countries, but it has been accepted in Switzerland for many years; it has been accepted in sbme of the states of the neighbouring Republic with a measure of success; it has been accepted by some of the western provinces; it is the law of the land in Australia and New Zealand, and we ourselves, sometimes refer matters .of municipal government to the people before enacting them. The other day we received as our honored guest one of the foremost statemen of the world. I refer to the right hon. Arthur James Balfour, who represents, I believe, in the Empire and in the world, the most enlightened conservatism that I know of. His noble language, the other day, establishes^ that fact. He, a Conservative, asserted his belief, his faith in democracy and in democratic rule. On the question of tariff reform which, a few years ago, agitated public opinion in Great Britain, the position taken by Mr. Balfour, which is well worth the consideration of my hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) was as follows:
The advantage of the referendum is this- that the issue is quite clear and quite precise. .	. The referendum has an enormous
advantage. It does not involve a general election; it does not involve all the personal bitterness inevitably involved in the contest between the two competitors for a seat; it does not carry with it a change of government ; and it does get a clear verdict from the people. .	. Nevertheless, I frankly say
that without question tariff reform is a great change. I admit that this election, or any election perhaps-certainly this election-cannot be described as taken upon tariff reform simply; but I have not the least objection to submit the principles of tariff reform to referendum.
If Mr. Balfour was willing to break away from the traditions of England and take a referendum on such a purely theoretical question as tariff reform, surely we in Canada, can afford to take' a referendum on the conscription of the yeomanry of this country. But Mr. Balfour is not alone of that view. Professor Dicey one of the highest authorities on constitutional government, has declared himself favourably on the principle of referendum in British affairs. Lecky, who is also one of the foremost authorities, on the British Government and constitution, in " Democracy and Liberty " volume I, p. 287 and following presents a most elaborate argument in favour of the referendum. I have prepared a short synopsis of it. The referendum would prevent the placing of the essential elements of the constitution at the mercy of a simple majority

in a single Parliament

a majority perhaps composed of heterogeneous and discordant factions combined for a party purpose without the direct and deliberate assent of the people. It seems as those words of his were uttered on this very question and under the circumstances ,of to-day. The referendum would have the immense advantage of disentangling issues, *separating the one great question from the many minor questions with which it may be mixed. Confused or blended issues aTe among the gravest political dangers of our time. Revolutionary and predatory (measures are less likely to be carried on their merits because their purposes have obtained a majority by joining with them a sufficient number of other measures appealing to different sections of the electorate. It would be a great gain to English politics if a capital question could be decided by the electorate on its own merits, on a direct and simple issue. If the nation is moving towards revolution it should at least do so with its eyes open and with a~ clear and deliberate intention. Such a vote would prove to be the most powerful bulwark against violent and dishonest change. It would bring into action the opinion of the great silent masses of the community ana reduce to their true proportion many movements to which party combinations or noisy agitations had given a wholly fictitious prominence. It would lift above the dominion of party a capital measure, and thus greatly increase the probability of its representing the genuine wishes of the electorate. It would enable the nation to reject a measure which it dislikes without destroying a ministry of which it approves. Democracy has been crowned king. The voice of the multitude is the ultimate court of appeal. It would be an appeal from a party majority, probably made up of discordant groups, to the genuine opinion of the country.
Besides Professor Dicey, Mr. Leeky and Mr. Balfour, we have another opinion, that of the right hon. leader of the Government on this question. The late, Mr. Monk once moved for a referendum on the naval question, to which a sub-amendment was moved by the present Prime Minister; this being lost, the right hon. the Prime Minister was given the privilege of voting for Mr. Monk's amendment for a referendum. Yes, he and all his followers, with the exception of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, voted for the leferendum.
If it was necessary to submit the naval policy of the Laurier Government to a referendum-a policy which did not involve conscription, a policy which had been dealt with by the Imperial Conferences of 1902 and 1909-surely, Sir, it is much more logical and much more urgent to submit to a referendum such a momentous question ae that of the conscription of the 'blood of the young men of this country, enacted by a moribund and unrepresentative Parliament.
I have trespassed too long on the time of the House, but I will say this in conclusion, and I say it with all the firmness and all the good faith that I can attach to solemn statement:	knowing the people of my
province to be above all things a law-abiding people, if a referendum is taken, whether it goes for or against conscription, the French-Canadians, who are the descendants of those who defended Canada in 1775, in 1812, will abide by the verdict of the majority. If conscription comes they will not have to be bullied or dragooned into the ranks, but will -obey the law and fight the battles of Canada as (valiantly as their fellow-men of a different race and a different creed.
